This game is totally not worth $10, but I can recommend it when it's on sale.
There are 40 levels. If you want the achievements, you'll need to play them again in hardcore mode.
The game is a marble game, so if you've never played one, you probably should.
Honestly, I don't know what else to put here. It's a short marble game. Some puzzles require you to think like a developer (also known as testing out the game's limits or cutting corners or being observant), some required above average reflexes, and there was this one visual bug on this one level (not game-breaking, just neat). Make sure you pay attention to the level tips, because there's no way to view them outside the level. The trading cards are kinda valuable. Some achievements shouldn't exist. That's about it.

I was looking for a game similar to super monkey ball. It's not quite monkey ball, but I did find it enjoyable. The marbles don't control like marbles you would expect in a marble game. The acceleration, deceleration, and momentum are completely different. The puzzles are very simple but get better later on into the game. The length of the levels tends to be short as well. My main complaint is the lack of a monkey ball expert or super expert equivalent. I feel like if the game had kept getting more levels, that would have happened. I just wish the levels tended to be a bit longer I was hoping for 2-4 minute levels instead of 30 second to 1 minute. This game would have really benefited from a community level editor. The music was very enjoyable and fit the game in my eyes.
It's pretty lame and definitely not worth 10$.

Lost Marbles is a great idea that is executed poorly. The core concept is clever; different marbles made out of different materials, being able to do different things in order to get all the marbles to the end of the level. Simple, all well and good. The problem is that it's a 3D platformer, and in the end, it doesn't realise the problems that 3D platformers face, meaning that it falls into a feeling of randomness in terms of its gameplay.
In several sections of the game, I died more times than I felt like I should have simply because I slid off a platform, or because I didn't get a feeling for the depth between two platforms (and the platforms aren't designed for the marble's maximum jump distance; meaning you can jump past the platform, which is infuriating in a 3D platformer where depth perception is an issue), or I didn't catch enough speed to get across a gap that I couldn't judge the width of. There were many parts in the game where it felt like you had to fight against the mechanics instead of working with them, simply because of the level design not being balanced fully around the "powers" that the marbles have at times. When the game itself is stripped down in the way that Lost Marbles is, where the mechanics and level design is all there is, and those then feel amateurish and mediocre at best... then the game is majorly flawed.
Honestly, this game is not worth the money or time. As someone who do seek to finish all games to the end, I couldn't even bother to do that with this game, despite it being so short. The game does function, at times it's even fun to play; but the flaws do weigh down the good parts, and in between the good and the bad the game is just... dull. In the end, there are a lot of games out there that have way better execution that this one, and you should probably skip over Lost Marbles.

I like it.
This game works well. Its ideas and elements flow together, and I like that.
It has 40 levels, and while that does make the playtime substantial, I feel like there could've been more. Something that this game would do well with is steam workshop custom map support. That could make the game a lot more fun.
The physics engine works pretty well. There's only one thing that I struggle to get used to, and that is how the marbles decelerate when I stop moving. They come to a stop much quicker than I expect, as I'm used to something similar to how marbles slow down in real life, so that's just something that I need to get used to.
One thing about this game that sort of left me unsatisfied me was the death animations. I expected that if I rolled a paper ball into fire, it would burn, and if I ran a rubber ball over some spikes, that the ball would pop, but instead, the ball just disappears, and a ghost-like skull just floats above it, and that just kind of seems lazy.
Other than that, the nature of the puzzles feels nice and smooth, and I do like hopping on and playing a quick permadeath on it, so I'd recommend it to anyone who likes a quick 3D puzzler.

Marble platformer games are almost a dying breed in this era of gaming, but when one comes around it usually becomes quite the unique and enjoyable experience. Lost Marbles, proves to be an example of that.
What I found most enticing about this game was the amount of collaborative effort between the three individual marbles, and how they work together to help reach the exit. Nearly all of the levels feature unique elements, and the developers did a great job making sure none of the marbles had a clear path to the exit without needing to contribute anything to to the map. They also did a great job making the 3 marbles unique from each other; you can definitely feel and notice the weight and speed difference between them.
While I found tons of enjoyment out of the game as a whole, there are still a couple things I personally had a little less fun with, one being the par times, which while I definitely know were fixed recently, still prove to be frustrating to beat later on. The only way I can describe the way the par times feel (at least only in the later half of the game) is that I have to speed run recklessly through the level with no room for hesitation. Thankfully the par times aren't required to beat in order to progress so I see it more of an optional thing to challenge myself with later on. The only other thing that bothered me were the graphics of the Menu GUI. As a graphic designer I find the use of the white and black drop shadows on the windows to be a bit awkward, and the 1 pixel stroke around the lettering is definitely not very appealing to the eye, but again that is just a very minor qualm that doesn't really affect the overall game too much.
Regardless of the menu graphics though, I found the game environment to be quite enticing. In spite of the unusual thick outlining around all of the objects, I felt that worked to the games favor because you can very clearly see what you can interact with without it detracting from anything. I also liked the attention to detail with the sound effects, especially that each marble has a different rolling sound.
Overall I found this game to be very enjoyable; I'm happy to have assisted with the developer in pushing a new update to enhance the gameplay, and the fixes he did very much show a noticeable improvement from the last big update.

Lost Marbles concept is pretty straightforward: control and guide marbles, from the beginning of a level to the end. There are three types of marbles you will control. First, a rubber marble that can jump, swim in water and survive electrical damage. Second, a paper marble that can change its size to fit into smaller spaces and moved away on wind. Third, a metal marble that can be affected by magnets, ignore damage from fire and spikes, and accelerate forward to break through barriers. All of the marbles must reach the end of any given level in order for the stage to be completed. The puzzles require coordination and straight up puzzle solving. The controls are incredibly simple: roll your ball with the WASD keys, and change your camera angle by moving the mouse. Beyond this, a hardcore mode is available, tasking you with having to complete the levels perfectly in a raw, while failures sending you back to the beginning of the previous level. Which can be very disappointing and annoying, but fun in some wicked sense of humor way. Lost Marbles is a solid, decently polished game that delivers some well crafted challenge. If you are on the hunt for a new puzzle game to challenge you, this one is at least worth a look. Overall, the game was pleasant, refreshing and frustrating.

Progress develops all spheres of our life - including games. How many titles and forgotten concept genres left behind me, a man who was born in the XXI century? The first serious RPGs, old school shooters, hardcore simulators, and so on. And it's very nice when developers make different adaptations, remasters, REDUX versions of old and not very games, re-think them, and give us a new gaming experience with old basics.
Breakout Invaders is a neoclassical Arkanoid. The gameplay here is simple - you control a miniature spaceship, your goal is to use balls to make a chop from the enemy and destroy the buildings, along the way upgrading the ship and moving on through more difficult maps.
To start, you need to mark the graphics. When creating games of such a small scale, without a large budget, you must first of all make a memorable and unusual design, rather than chasing technical innovations in the form of 3D graphics and colorful effects. The game feels like a matinee in a kindergarten - the same colorful, bright, rich picture without a knowing of limits and any desire to do something unique.
The technical aspect of the game is also not impressive. Crashes to the desktop, bugs (including graphic ones), unregulated screen resolution, bug with saves (which deleted my progress after an hour of the game), and so on. The game is full of flaws which is very disturbing to play, and most importantly - spoils the impression of the gameplay.
The music is normal, somewhat relaxing, and perfectly copes with the function of the gameplay ambient, but no more.
The gameplay here is various, and it is very good. Despite what I said above - Arkanoid was redone so that the player does not bother with the gameplay, constantly supplementing it with additional modes and elements of the game. Uprading the ship, destroying buildings, enjoing the classic levels of arkanoid, improved, and most importantly interesting levels with their goals and objectives. The maps are as many as 100 pieces, so it takes a long time to play, but it does not tire out like in other indie games. This is what the 1986 game needed - it was just finished and made more interesting, vigorous and fun.

Прогресс идёт, развиваются все наши сферы жизни - в том числе и развлечения, игры. Сколько тайтлов и забытых концепт-жанров осталось позади меня, человека, который родился в XXI веке? Первые серьёзные РПГ, олдскульные шутеры, хардкорные симуляторы, и так далее. И очень приятно, когда разработчики делают различные адаптации, ремастеры, REDUX-версии старых и не очень игр, переосмысливают их, и дают нам новый игровой опыт со старыми основами.
Breakout Invaders - это неоклассический Арканоид. Геймплей здесь простой - вы управляете миниатюрным космическим кораблём, ваша цель - с помощью шаров делать отбивную из противника и разрушать постройки, попутно прокачивая корабль и продвигаясь дальше по более сложным картам.
Для начала, нужно отметить графику. При создании игр такого небольшого масштаба, без большого бюджета необходимо сделать в первую очередь запоминающийся и необычный дизайн, а не гнаться за техническими новшествами в виде 3D графики и разноцветных эффектов. Игра ощущается как утренник в детском саду - такая же цветастая, яркая, насыщенная картинка без чувства меры и какого-нибудь желания сделать что-то уникальное.
Технический аспект игры тоже не впечатляет. Вылеты, баги (в том числе и графические), нерегулируемое разрешение экрана, баганая система сохранений (которая откинула мой прогресс спустя час игры), и так далее. Игра наполнена недоработками и мелкими огрехами, что сильно мешает играть, а самое главное - портит впечатление от игрового процесса.
Музыка обычная, в некоторой степени расслабляющая, и отлично справляющаяся с функцией геймплейного эмбиента, но не более того.
Геймплей здесь разнообразный, и это очень порадовало. Несмотря на то, что я сказал выше - арканоид был переделан так, чтобы игроку не надоедал игровой процесс, постоянно разбавляя его дополнительными режимами и элементами. И прокачка корабля, и уничтожение построек, и классические уровни арканоида, и улучшенные, а самое главное интересные уровни со своими целями и задачами. Карт целых 100 штук, так что проходить игру нужно долго, но это не утомляет как в других инди-играх. Это то, что нужно было игре 1986 года - её просто доработали и сделали интереснее, энергичнее и занимательнее.

Breakout Invaders is a mash up of both Space Invaders and Breakout. If you are not familiar with those titles one is a vertical shoot em up and  the other is pretty much reverse Pong in where you try to break all the blocks and not let the ball pass your goal. There are 100 levels and each level usually changes how the game plays. One mission you will be tasked with breaking all the blocks and in the next you may be tasked with defending blocks from aliens using your ball and lasers as a weapon. Lasers are used by either right clicking or using the alt key and can be used to destroy blocks or damage enemies though whether you have unlimited ammo depends level from level. You also have a missile which causes far more damage and has splash damage but you can only carry up to 10. In later levels they introduce metal gates that won't allow you to shoot blocks and must use a ball to reach them.
That is easier said than done. The physics in Breakout Invaders are completely insane and have no logic behind them at times. Your ball is the bounciest thing in the universe and hitting it with the edge of your paddle does not bounce it to the side like you would expect. It's a hard thing to explain but imagine playing Pong and the ball always going straight up instead of being able to bounce it off the sides of the screen when you learn to hit it properly.  Unlike Breakout or Space Invaders this has a pinball like perspective to the maps instead of a simple 2D plane, so that adds some more complexity to it. Destroying castles and cites is great fun even though most of the times you will break blocks by chance instead of skill. Unfortunately later on they introduce small pipes that you must shoot your ball into to reach an area but the controls and physics are just not up to par to require the precision they so those end up being a pain.
You can control the game with either your mouse or your arrow keys but the mouse is way too sensitive for my liking. It works perfectly fine with the arrows keys but in some levels you are required to use the mouse which is pretty annoying. Which brings me to my biggest gripe with the game. Every level seems to have some kind of cheap gimmick like having 10 balls on screen for 2 minutes or having to destroy some blocks but having one paddle and goal on each side of the screen, making it feel like a game of Warlords that makes you have to control all players at once . The game is at it's best when it has you just breaking blocks yet every level has some kind of nuisance to break the flow once you start to actually have fun. It really makes it feel like a collection of mini games instead of modes built around the basic mechanics of Breakout and would have benefited from having them as extra features instead of being forced into the base game.
Another good portion of the game will have you fighting the aliens from Space Invaders and these are in my opinion the worst part of the game. Your paddle is way too large and makes avoiding projectiles a real pain plus you still have to worry about your ball. It's like being the fat guy in a game of paintball and having to text your boss in the middle of a gunfight. You do usually have infinite ammo for your laser but when you are down to the last few aliens they become extremely bullet spongy. It is insane how many hits they take and I actually thought my game was glitched until one of the three finally exploded. That is due to the tacked on upgrade system this game has. You will need to collect money to buy new ships or to upgrade your firepower. The problem is the game is incredibly stingy with money and the only way to get more is completing a level so you have two options, either grind some prior levels or deal with it. With that and having a gimmick every level it is like the devs think we have the attention span of a newt  and need some kind of motive to play the game instead of it simply playing for the fun of it like say the two games they so proudly mention.
Both Space Invaders and Breakout were about skill. They were both based around improving the player, not the ship with extra firepower or the paddle with more speed. They gave you all the tools you  needed from the get go and designed the game around that. Breakout Invader on the other hand simply beefs up the enemies and hopes you spent your limited cash correctly if you don't want to spend the next couple of minutes slowly chipping off the enemies health. It honestly would have been a better game if you had a single ship, no upgrades and optional game modes like the games it was inspired by. Moving on from that rant, there are other power-ups besides rockets and lasers.  There are meteors that will destroy parts of the map, items that either shrink or increase your paddle and one that makes balls move faster. One small gripe is that items come down too slowly and would benefit from a bit more speed going down. Can be a bit bothersome waiting for it to makes its way down the screen while keeping track of the ball.
Environments are not pretty bland and takes quite some time to see any new ones. Music is a mixed bag, it ranges from good to terrible. Some sound effects sound right out of the late 70's which is nice. It was a fun game when it played like Breakout but with power ups, though every other gimmick was sub-par. If you are a fan of Space Invaders I wouldn't bother with this game. If you are a fan of Breakout there is a bit of fun to be had here but the good will ultimately be outweighed due to having to put up with gimmick after gimmick just to get to the next level that plays like Breakout. It is such an annoying design decision, it is like playing one level of one game, switching to a few other games and then going back to the one you actually like. Having them as different game modes instead of lumping them together to have “100 levels” would have been preferred.  It's a shame, it could have been a decent little throwback but the devs spread themselves too thin and choose quantity over the quality of the gameplay.

This game is pretty bad, but for $2 it's hard to argue with. I don't know how many people these days have played or even heard of Ballance, and I have no idea how many other games are similar to Ballance or what Ballance got its ideas from, but Puzzle Ball feels like a worse made version of some of those other marble puzzle games.
Either way Ballance is rather old, and doesn't have a level editor. The puzzles in Puzzle Ball are pretty fun though extremely easy, but with the level editor the possibilities are endless but since I'm not a creative type I doubt I'll see much use out of it.
What makes the game bad? The music is terrible, a mouse cursor always flashes in the middle of the screen, the menus overlap, there's no 'next level' option when you beat a level, you can't actually close menus in 2-player mode without exiting the stage or restarting the level, deaths are rather meaningless since there's no lives or penalty that I can see, and only about half of the vital text is in English, the other half in Dutch or something. This made the tutorial totally useless, but the idea is pretty easy: use WASD or the arrow keys to guide your ball to the end using two other ball types (a stone and a paper mache ball) to solve the various puzzles. Each ball is better at different things, like paper being able to go over water (but wood can't float enough apparently) and stone being able to do some heavy hitting and fall through glass.

What's good about it? The controls are good, the graphics are good, the puzzles are good, and this game is cheap as Puzzle Balls. --OVERVIEW--
I just got this game on release day, and I must, say, it's surprising! Puzzle Ball is, in essence, a spiritual successor to marble-based games like Marble Blast Gold, Ballance and Marble Madness. Being a lover of Marble Blast Gold, I thought that this couldn't hurt and gave it a try. After playing with a few of the scenario levels and checking out the level editor, I must say that this game is amazingly fun for 3 dollars. This game is not as much of a skill platformer as others in its genre, but is more of a puzzle, like the name implies. Figuring out the order in which to accomplish challenges for a high score is important, as some points can be permanently missed if you don't do them at the right times. However, there is never so much chalenge that you will get angry at the game, as the game does live up to its "casual" tag This, the beautiful graphics, and the relaxing music combine to create a surprisingly fun experience, as watching each levels' mechanisms come to life is fascinating, and there is some satisfaction in completing each level.
--THE EDITOR--
In addition, the level editor is quite easy to use, as the description states. It is a simple "pick block and place" style editor. However, the camera and controls of the editor are a bit weird, so there is definitely room for improvement there. Other than that, there isn't too much for me to say about the level editor, as I'm not into taht sort of thing.
>NOTE: There is a "level budget," so you cannot make infinitely big levels! :(
--MENUS--
This is where my criticisms start. After launching the game, you will be treated to a small graphic informing you of the controls. There seems to be no way to bring this up again besides restarting the game. After dealing with the graphic, you will be treated to a menu with no logo and four buttons: "Levels," "Editor," "Options" and "Quit." Clicking "Levels" takes you to a bland screen with the 11 scenario leves shown, with the options to look at user levels. Clicking "Editor" throws you straight into the editor with no options or preparation screen. Selecting "Options" brings you to an options screen where you can edit your screen resolution, quality (idk what this exactly means), your languages (choices of English, Russian, and Dutch), something called "Image Resolution" (I really have no idea what this does), your sound/music volumes, whether to be fullscreen/windowed, bloom, and SSAO. There is no way to rebind key controls, although they are standard (WASD) and you shouldn't have trouble with them. While the menus certainly are functional, they are bland and lack depth; but as this is a 3 dollar game, it is acceptable.
--PROS--
>Interesting gameplay
>Very nice graphics
>Relaxing music
>Infinite replayability with the level editor
>Good learning curve
--CONS--
>Only 11 built-in levels
>Lame menus
>Some typical functionality missing (rebinding controls, advanced graphics, etc.)
>Small music selection
--VERDICT--
>9/10<

At the time of writing, I'm playing a lot of games that are quite heavy on the game-mechanics side of things (HeXen, Unreal, Prince of Persia, STALKER) or story (KoTOR II, Mafia).
For me, this is the perfect cooldown from endless dialog trees, droves of enemy types and labyrinths upon labyrinths of levels. Just shoot the on-rails moving balls with your static frog turret so the ball colours match and clear the level before the time runs out. You have some fairly straightforward powerups like slow moving balls and reverse movement direction, then there's accuracy and explosion. Nothing too fancy, but it's so effective as a time killer.
The music is also very fitting, just hype enough to keep your brain firing but still inocuous enough to not make you nervous (unless you're near death, then the music changes and it's meant to make you nervous).
There's an "adventure" mode, where you complete levels by hitting a certain points threshold, and survival mode with four difficulty levels where the balls just keep coming until you lose.
Don't let this fool you into thinking the game is easy, however. It has that patented PopCap balance of challenging, addictive and still enjoyable. Like I said, I love to play it when I don't feel like watching a movie or series but I don't feel like playing some hardcore 90s FPS either.
The only downside is that the levels in this game are saved as 640x480 JPEG files, so there is absolutely no way to change the resolution, let alone aspect ratio. On my 1366x768 laptop screen, it's not as bad, but I imagine it would be pretty jarring on a 1080 or even 1440 screen.
All in all, it's a shame they didn't update the visuals or even just upscale the whole thing, otherwise this game would be perfect - it's a steal during sales anyway, so even with the dated visuals, I recommend it wholeheartedly.

As one of the PopCap classics from the mid 2000s, Zuma brought me and my family counless fun hours for over a decade.
The gameplay is simple, match three balls of the same color together and get combos, chains or collect randomly appearing coins to increase the yielded score.
There's also a couple of power-ups which appear occasionally which can help you, such as reversing the balls movement, stopping their movement entirely, causing a big explosion which destroys its surrounding balls and an aim help which lets you shoot your balls quicker.
This game is brought down in two modes, the Adventure and a Gauntlet mode (which is pretty much a survival mode).
-The Adventure Mode is a stage-to-stage Level Rush where you have to score a specific amount of points to stop more balls from spawning and then clear the screen to get to the next stage.
All this is split into multiple different worlds with more colors to appear the deeper you get.
-The Gauntlet Mode allows you to play any stage you beat in the Adventure Mode and attempt to survive as long as you can, while attempting to score as much points as possible.
One thing I'd like to mention is the games modability, yes I'm serious!
If you look into the local files, you notice that most image and audio files (except of the background-music unfortunately) use default file extensions and formatting.
This means you can easily replace game files and inplement your own files if you want an entirely new Zuma experience!
I cannot tell you if any format works, but as long as you covert your files into the same extension as they were in Zuma (most of them are .jpg, .gif and .ogg), it should work just fine. (atleast it did for me and a friend of mine)
You might want to backup your save file though prior to the modding, just in case something goes majorly wrong which forces you to re-install the game, thus as always mod at your own risk!
The only problems I have are:
-Maximum resolution of 640x480, which you can get used to in fullscreen, but can cause trouble when playing in windowed mode. (see next point)
-The game does not force the cursor inside the games window when you don't use fullscreen, hence you can click outside the window accidentaly and not shoot while playing. Trust me, this happens more than you'd wish!
-I honestly believe it's not worth the full price of €5 any more. This game came out 14 years ago and its successor is avaiable for the same price, offering way more.
BUT:
If this game IS on sale, I can only recommend this to anyone as it's a very addictive experience which first up seems very simple, but gets more complex when you get to later stages, both in Adventure and in Gauntlet.
The graphics are ok for its time while the music fits the atmosphere perfectly.
Even if my playtime on Steam isn't that high yet, I can promise you my (and also my parents) time spent into this game would exceed your expectations.

Zuma Deluxe is a puzzle game where you control a rotating from from a top down view in what looks like an ancient Aztec/Mayan temple of sorts.  There is a track on the screen that has multicolored balls moving through the track.  The objective is to shoot colored balls from the mouth of the rotating frog onto balls along the track.  Once three or more colors are formed together from a ball from the frog's mouth, the balls disappear.  But watch out!  There is an end to the track!  So as your balls move along this track, if you don't lessen the line of the track, then you could easily find yourself in the losers pit.
My big deal is that I have played this game countless times before.  I didn't want to play through every single level ever all over again.  No big deal!  I played the first and second level, and the AI recognized my skill level and asked me if I would like to go to a level more fitting for my skill level.  Nothing makes me happier when a game recognizes my ability to play at a higher difficulty, and tailors itself to that difficulty.
Make no mistake.  This game isn't a serious buy.  If you want something to pass the time, or get bored by the expensive AAA titles, pick up this game and give it a whirl.  If you hate time passing puzzle games, then you might not like this game.  I will never uninstall this title though.  Never.  Not even to make room for Deus Ex: Human Revoution.

is a small step up, and acceptable for less-choosy players, but still not entirely choiceworthy.

Like all
titles, the core "vertical Zuma" gameplay is still there, but 3 goes far beyond 2 in adding extras.  There's a puzzle mode, a hectic timed-defense mode, an "Onslaught" mode where you try to play Luxor while simultaneously shooting down pop-up barriers that shorten the track, a river-crossing mode that blends
mechanics with
level design.  There are plenty of powerups, and by collecting coins, you can purchase upgrades for your favourites.  Other targets appearing from time to time grant score and coin bonuses or unlock bonus levels.
Even with all I've mentioned
still isn't the most feature-laden casual game on the market in 2017, but there's enough content and variety there that it doesn't feel barren, outdated or too limited.  For the action-casual player,
will still be quite satisfactory, all the more so if you catch it on a good sale.

A marble game, where you have to collect Gems leading to the end, in pretty hard levels, and where most of the fun lies in breaking the game in amazing ways.
This game has the advantage of being amongst the few marble games on Steam, and it's actually miles better than its predecessor, Spectraball.  There's little you can do, but that's not a bad thing, as you'll be navigating your ball on thin platforms and scale up arrangements of beams, shifting gravity along the way.  Collecting Gems makes even the more open levels linear, but that's an ok enough goal, although it could've been nice if you could see the ghost of the next Gem; you can't collect them out of order.  This game delivers on "good" difficulty for the most part.
Well, almost, the jumping mechanics sort of doesn't work, pressing the jump button once makes the ball do one of the pathetic jumps I've ever seen, it feels unnatural; you can do a Double Jump, but it's a strange learning curve that might annoy people, as it did for me.  The Magnet Ball, which is used a few times through the game, doesn't really work as advertised, it sometimes sticks off walls and makes gravity shift in unexpected ways, it's almost a better thing to abuse the game's physics (mmh...).  The speed boosters also doesn't really work well, I would go up the ramp after getting the speed, and then I wouldn't get any height.  You'd also have to go though Portals, which does keep you momentum, but there were times where you would go trough one and it dumps you over a small platform, and as the camera freaks out over the sudden change, you would often fall off without being able to do anything.
So, it utterly fails at basic things (much like Spectraball now that I think about it), so why am I still giving it a positive review?  Well, as I've said, you could abuse the physics of the game.  For one thing, if you rapidly press the jump button, and I mean Mary Canary fast, the ball makes amazing leaps that break levels, a freaking lot.  Bumping on walls and ceilings also resets the "Double Jump counter", which means that you can do wall jumps and scale up things.  Additionally, the Gems have a rather big hitbox, so you could cut corners by being on the opposite sides.  It's surprisingly fun breaking the game like that, and it shaves off a lot of time in trying to do the best time on the leaderboards, for each levels.  The camera also stays perfectly fine on normal instances, despite the Portal incidents, and there weren't really a part of the game where it was being a total meanie.
There are 20 normal levels, and 3 challenge levels, the last of which really didn't thrilled me, but it's there.
So yeah, Dexterity Ball 3D is quite an oddball, it doesn't really work right most of the time, and yet can be very fun if you abuse its physics like I did.  Dunno,
, and a nice and quick diversion, although perhaps tread carefully, I'm only enjoying this because I'm freaking bizarre.

TL;DR: Dirt cheap and a lot of fun, Zuma’s Revenge is definitely worth picking up by anyone looking for a relaxed, casual gaming experience.

Zuma’s Revenge is a fun, casual game similar to the arcade classic Puzzle Bobble. Despite its early ease and colorful cartoonish graphics, Zuma’s Revenge does actually get pretty challenging towards the end of the game’s campaign. You’ve been warned!

Personally, I would say that Zuma's Revenge is one of PopCap's best games ever made (Not very far behind Plants vs. Zombies). Zuma's Revenge is a very intriguing puzzle game that anyone can enjoy regardless of age or interests. This game is a puzzle game about blowing bubbles and matching 3 or more colors. Your goal is to fill a gauge located in the top of the screen while the balls roll closer into a skull's mouth. If the balls reach the skull, you've failed. Getting point bonuses helps fill the gauge faster. Once you fill the gauge, new balls stop rolling in, and you'll most likely finish the stage shortly after. Because there is so much to cover in this game, I'll review the game modes individually.
Zuma's Revenge offers a great adventure mode. The game starts out straightforward and simple, but it continues to get harder as you progress. The difficulty curve this game offers is done very well. As the game gets harder, the generated balls go from 4 colors to 5 up to 6 individual ball colors. Making matches becomes harder as you progress in the game. The bosses you fight along your adventure are really enjoyable.
Challenge mode will add plenty of hours of enjoyment to your experience. Instead of filling a gauge in challenge mode, your goal is to score a certain amount of points in a limited amount of time. Multiplier powerups show up while you play, so aim to acquire those to increase your score. Taking on these challenges is not only challenging but really fun to play.
These two challenges are both unlocked after completing adventure mode. Heroic Frog is a more difficult replay of adventure mode, and it will occupy you for plenty of time.
Iron Frog Gauntlet consists of 10 stages, each requiring a lot of skill and patience to beat. Play at your own risk!
Be sure to get Zuma's Revenge; it's a great value and only costs $4.99! You won't regret playing it!

Pop Cap games are truly a mixed bag. On one hand, you could get lucky with Plants Vs. Zombies or Peggle. But, on the other, you could be playing Zuma's Revenge. Before continuing, I would like to note that this review is coming from solely playing the adventure mode. Zuma's Revenge's adventure mode has you playing as a frog on an island, making your way through on your adventure.
The gameplay seems to be simple, Zuma having a color ball and having to match three or more of the same color of ball on the track before the balls reach a certain point to which you have to restart the round. On paper, this seems quite simple but the game needs polish as it becomes frustrating when the game solely relies on luck to win the round. The music to the game is simple but, unfortunately, lacking. The same song always plays, allowing for no diversity and not giving the player any reason to keep listening.
In adventure mode, the frog most fight bosses but it doesn't feel like there are any at all. For the most part, the bosses are simple, the only boss which is noticable is the last one because of it's three-stage gauntlet.
To wrap up, Zuma's Revenge seems to be attempting to ride on the success of Peggle, a game which came out two years prior. However, where Peggle is both skill intensive and luck intensive, Zuma's Revenge simply relies on luck to get through. I did put in almost eight hours playing this game but that wasn't because I was having fun, that's because luck wasn't on my side. When the right set-up and power-ups came up, I was able to finally get past a stage that troubled me, no skill involved. If you have the money and would like to play a mindless game, buy Peggle instead.

In grand Popcap tradition, Zuma's Revenge is a simple game to learn, but exciting and satisfying to play and play and play.  The premise has a line of multi-colored marbles inching their way along a pre-defined path towards an ultimate drop-dead point and you have to shoot similar colored marbles at the line in order to create matches of at least three marbles.  Different bonuses will allow greater control over the advancing line, but the real progress comes from simply being dextrous enough to notice the matches and quickly fire accurately.  The game is relatively stress free until the final levels when the game starts throwing interlocking looped paths which block your ability to manipulate the entire line and forcing you to act quick and precise to keep things managable.  At certain points the game changes and you face off against different "boss" characters which employ subtle variations to the game techniques.  The experience prooves to be very satisfying and quite rewarding.

On A Roll 3D is a platformer game that surprised me.  From the looks of it, this game looked like something someone threw together real quick, and just happened to get it greenlit on Steam.  However, I gave it a fair chance, thanks to the Steam Summer Sale, and really enjoyed it.
In On A Roll 3D, you play as a ball, and simply roll to the end using basic platforming skills.  Each world has various different mechanics added to it to make the game feel fresh on every new world, and the level design is really solid.  If you've ever played a Sonic the Hedgehog game, the level design for On A Roll 3D very much resemble these games.  The controls are very responsive, and have never failed me in my entire playthrough of the game.
Graphically, the game looks like an older PC game from back in the day.  It doesn't look too good, but the simplicity of the game gives this graphic style a bit of charm as well.  The soundtrack is pretty bland, with only a handful of memorable tracks (mainly the title screen music).
While the game is pretty short, with my playthrough lasting close to 2 hours, On A Roll 3D is definitely worth purchasing, if you're a fan of platforming games.  I feel that this game is worth $4, and I can't help but feel that lots of people are going to miss out on this title.  The only reason I wouldn't recommend this game, is if the graphics don't look appealing to you, or if you simply don't like the platformer genre.  If you're still on the fence about On A Roll 3D, wait for the game to be at least $2-$3 before purchasing.

PRE-UPDATE: A classic 2D side-scroller with 3D graphics (2.5D?) with some unique twists thrown into the mix creating a fresh and fun platforming experience.
And although it does use elements seen in most platformers what's wrong with keeping the tradition if it's not broken?
Now I have played the original On A Roll on XBLA and so far On A Roll 3D isn't as difficult as its predecessor, but don't let the game's bright, colorful art-style fool you as it may provide challenge in the later levels.
Which is another thing, this game, despite its simplistic graphics is bright and colorful and makes the game pop (which is always a plus in my book as most games these days have a dull color palette), the controls are very tight and responsive (although controller support isn't the best but still works great) and probably one of the best aspects of the game is its soundtrack, my goodness...this game's soundtrack is super catchy and upbeat, drawing you closer to the game.
POST-UPDATE: The new update for the game basically improves EVERYTHING from a more refined interface, to adjustable resolutions (the pre-update version of the game was locked at 1280x720) to a major overhaul to the game's visuals (pre-update looked fine but post-update made a lot of changes such as better water, shadows and other stuff) and the best part: DEFINIABLE CONTROLS, that means players who use their Xbox One/PlayStation 4 (or other PC gamepad) can finally set up their controller to function properly with the game. (pre-update controls still made you pause the game with the escape key and a few other keyboard inputs and pre-update controls made every button on the game controller perform the same action, BIG thanks to Battenberg Software for answering my question on controller mapping!)
If you like what I say about the game AND is a fan of classic 2D (2.5D?) platformers, then I strongly recommend this game!
P.S. DLC for this game is on its way, so if you're the kind of gamer who likes to get the most gametime out of a single game, then this'll be right up your alley!

is a simple retro platformer where you roll around trying to get to the end goal while collecting stars. If you think that sounds an awful lot like Sonic the Hedgehog you’d be right. This game is clearly inspired by old school Sonic games, from the level designs and graphics to the way bosses are destroyed. This a fun game in its own right and also pretty darn cute as well. There is however no story to be told.
You roll around, that’s about it. While you roll you have to collect stars and avoid dangerous death spikes, lasers and the like. There are also enemies along the way but you can easily jump on their heads and dispatch of them, the thing I had the biggest issue is was jumping onto small platforms and making sure I didn’t roll off since it is a ball and balls tend to roll. Your ball does not have any special powers or abilities which is a shame. A little something to spice things up every now and again would be fun. My favorite part of the gameplay was the puzzle aspect thrown in. Door in the way? You have to hit the switch or put something on top of it to get through.
I used a game controller to play the game and the responses were good. The only issue I had was that I could not find a button on my controller that would pause the game, I still had to use my keyboard for that. The retro feel of the game is really compliment by being able to use the controller. I also just figured out after over two hours of play that you can change the color of the ball so I made mine pink.
For me the graphics reminded me too much of Sonic the Hedgehog, like the first level looks strikingly similar to Green Hill Zone. However, the graphics aren’t so much of a direct copy and more of homage, that being said I do think the graphics could have been polished a bit more. The graphics are more akin to a Playstation One game than what I would expect in 2016. While graphics aren’t everything and this game is fun either way, they could have invested a little more into it. The audio is fine, though, the levels have catchy tunes and I had no issue there at all.
+ The game is very cheap.
+ Offers a good amount of gameplay for the price, game has six levels with three areas each plus a boss battle each time.
+ Overall presentation looks good.
+ It has trading cards.
- Only one play mode, no time trials or hidden areas that I could find.
- While the graphics weren’t bad they could have been better, the menu interfaces were also simplistic.
I do recommend this game to players who enjoy platformers, the game has a nice price tag and is well made. It’s fun, colorful and has great controls. This game also has achievements which are relatively easy to collect which is another draw. Buy it, play it and enjoy it you won’t regret it.

Windows 98 I've missed you... This game looks straight out the late 90's like PC shareware/demoware. It brings nostalgia to my very early encounters with windows 98 and it's plethora of low quality games and shovelware, and it plays like a game from around then. If this puts you off, this is definately not for you in the slightest. If you are not interested in playing something that doesn't feel new or even polished then this is also not for you. This is for people who understand that it's a small game with low quality cheesy textures and simple (but sometimes clunky feeling) controls. It will also help if you have played windows games from the 90's.
There are still small points in the game where it incorporates stuff from the 21st century, the shadows are pretty nice and when the camera rotates round as you move round a corner (pretty sure this happens like in the second half) it's something quite surreal and contradicting to the debatably eye-sore 90's style.
A few things to outline
- It took just over 2 hours to complete it start to finish. So expect play times around that, probably less if you're not as crap as me. I'd say between 1 1/2 hours to 2 is a reasonable guesstimate. I have not completed 100% achievements thus far and however the remainder of achievements I haven't completed is the time trial for the first level (which will probably take a few tries to crack) and the grindy achievements (get x score, collect x stars). The majority were collected through a straight playthrough. This could add another hour or so to play time. There is also 4 challenges on each levels (collect all stars, kill all enemies, don't die, don't get hit) which add to the replayability of the game but there's nothing really outside of just having a optional challenge that makes you want to do that. It does boost your score though.
- The controls are just the arrow keys however some of the controlling of the ball is a bit clunky and hard to grasp i.e. jumping isn't as sensitive as I'd want it to be and therefore precise jumping could be difficult sometimes. It does keep with the 90's windows platforming kind of games where controlling was far from perfect, so I guess it just adds more 90's. The levels aren't that difficult though so it's not too frustrating and the game isn't ruined by it either.
- Again don't expect major graphical content in it. Unless you have a 90's texture fetish.
Overall the game is pretty fun. It's nothing spectacular and it feels like 90's shovelware but I got some fun out of it. I personally wouldn't recommend it at full price though (I got it in a bundle, but a sale would suffice too), unless you understand the above points and like what you see. It'd be more suitable at half of it personally but with 100% achievements and everything completed you'd struggle to not find 3+ hours in it and £1/hour is usually a good ratio...

On A Roll is a short, low budget 2.5D platformer with obvious Sonic the Hedgehog influences. To the game's credit, it manages to incorporate elements of the Sonic games without ever feeling like a clone. It's definitely more inspiration than copying wholesale. The controls are also spot on. Movement with a 360 controller feels very tight and precise, and I never had trouble getting my character where I intended for it to be. Graphics are a big area where this game falls short. It doesn't look quite as bad in motion as the trailer makes it look, but that's not exactly a big compliment. The use of simple shapes for characters feels lazy, and the background elements aren't much better. On top of not having well put together graphics, I've also encountered some very obvious shadow glitching through large sections of the game. Not sure if this is a universal problem or specific to my rig, it doesn't break the experience, but it definitely doesn't add to the feeling of this being a well made and polished game.
Level design is actually quite solid, surprisingly so given how low budget the game feels. There's a mix of straightforward platforming and light physics puzzles. I'm not generally a fan of puzzle platformers, but here those elements are pretty innocuous. It's genuinely a fun game to play and there's far worse platformers on Steam. Music is decent too, if repetitive. The light and cutesy tone of the soundtrack fits with the feel of the game. The game only has partial controller support out of the box for a 360 controller, which is hard to forgive in a 2015 game, especially a platformer. The majority of the game can be handled with a controller just fine, but using menus and resetting the positions of movable objects both require a keyboard.
On A Roll made me smile, which is more than I can say for a lot of games in my library, even ones that are objectively better than this. If you grew up playing 2.5D games like Pandemonium, you should get a kick out of it. The game touches on nostalgia buttons that I didn't realize I had, and while the execution could use improvement, seeing an homage to that style of game feels good. It's only a few hours long, but for the very modest price that seems fair. For many people, the low quality graphics and being yet another puzzle platformer on Steam is going to be a dealbreaker, but if you've read this far and are still actually interested, you could definitely do a lot worse for your money. On A Roll may not be winning any game of the year awards, but it is enough fun to be worth looking past the flaws, especially if you're nostalgic for PS1 era 2.5D platformers.

TL;DR 5/10 A 1-track forced development of a civilization. Turn-based exponential clicker game.
5/10?  That is not great. Why am I still recommending it?  Well--I enjoyed myself for what it was.
As another reviewer warned before I played, this game plays like a clicker game, except turn-based.  Like all clicker games, the game goes through obscene levels of growth.  The result is that all of the action and growth that were done previously are quickly made irrelevant by the present state of growth.
The first time I played, I layed out a carefully managed plan of my resources.  Timed events occurred expecting me to be at a certain level of the growth curve.  I failed most of the challenging event (invading civilizations) because I thought that I could play the game at my own pace.  Since I conceded each of these overly unfair wars, none of my people died, and I was allowed to continue with a 40% reduction rate of some resource.  So, I lasted through half the game until the Huns came in and utterly wiped me out even with conceding the war.  During this first playthrough at my own managed pace, the game would feel sorry for me at certain checkpoints.  At least 8 different times, the game simply said, "Your neighbors are progressing well; so you benefit from the collective prosperity. Here is a reward of XX population, XX money, XX culture, XX army."  Literally 4 huge boosts to my present inventories of resources to try to level the playing field for where the game expected me to be.
Like other clicker games, your own army is irrelevant (when playing Athens, not Sparta). They participate, grow, and die in wars--but they are only meaningful as 5% of your army strength.  Your power comes from allying with neighbors and using their armies (20% of them) through treaty.  So, often, your army is your least important resource.  (The booster %bonuses to your army are very important, because they apply to your allied army)
Since it is a clicker game but turn-based, growth is mandatory at a certain time pace.  You must grow your population as fast as possible.  You keep them fed, while boosting 4 other resources--Production, Culture, Gold, with Army mostly irrelevant.  The only way to grow those resources is by allocating your population to each of the various tasks, fully changable each turn.
The second playthrough, I knew and could anticipate the non-random pre-timed events.  You shift your population into growing whichever resource is more important for the temporary challenge of the time.
The Production resource will purchase booster Buildings for your civilation layed out in a progressive tree of choices (along with a maintence fee to manage from your Gold resource.)  Culture will purchase boosters from a progressive Technology tree.  Both trees are mostly an illusion of choice.  You cannot purchase anything other than 2 or 3 options, and you are forced to purchase the other options soon afterwards.  Especially in the Technology tree, you are not allowed to purchase a more important technology from a different branch of study--the game forces you to purchase the remaining options first from earlier availability.  So, your only choice is what exact order of purchasing do you make in a forced, linear consumption track.
Many random events occur over the course of the 280-330 turn game.  "Here are some free armies."  "Here is some free culture."  "A city was poisoned; XX population die."  In a progressive game, these one time events are manageable and mostly shrugged off as a 1-3 turn delay.  However, I just hit mid-game the Starvation problem again.  You must have your farmers keep up with your growing population; yet because of the controlled expansion of farmers by the purchased Technology and Buildings, they can be maxed out.  So, my population got slightly ahead, with no ability to increase my farmers yet.  So, a few people die off and the population returns to an equilibrium of sustainability, right? WRONG !!  No joke--0.05% 100/200K of my people starved.  So, the game presents 3 punishments:  Give up some Culture growth for 10 turns, Spend an exhorbant amount of your Gold balance, OR murder 30% of your population.  OK--fine.  I took the Culture punishment.  However, next turn, the same problem is still there with no ability to rectify the food with increased farmers.  Again, 96/200K of my people die.  The game forces one of the remaining 2 choices of punishment.  So, after a few turns, the game forces you to murder 30% of your population because 0.05% were dying.
This kind of absurdity is the norm for this flawed game.  Well, I suppose it is similar to real life.  In RL, you planned and managed your resources, got an education, worked hard at a vocation.  Guess what?  Today, a truck hit you OR you got fingernail cancer.  You may not be dead, but which crippling result will you now manage for the rest of your life?
Grow your civilization along the path that the game expected, not much deviation is allowed.  Do this, and you will win the full achievements.  Almost.  Now do it one more time with the other Home city. (Athens or Sparta)
FATAL FLAWS:
#1 When conquering a city, you must beat them 3 times.  However, after each fight your armies lose an appropriate number in the fight.  However, for the target city, their armies magically respawn instantly.  Did they enlist more from the population?  -9M population, +16K army.
#2 When trading, other bonuses stack onto your commodity trades.  Unfortunately, this means that it makes sense to ONLY BUY when trading.  The bonuses do not boost your return of gold when selling.
Pay no more than $1.25 on sale for this.

Many people seem to be complaining about Marble Age being a "glorified Flash game". Well, it really quite literally is, considering that is the technology it uses (and you can find an earlier position in the series on those Flash games websites like Kongregate). But this isn't really a problem. In fact, The Binding of Isaac was a Flash game, too, and so what?
No, the problem with this game lies in its mechanics. The simplicity, combined with cute graphics, pretty nice music, and semi-educational content would have actually made it a great little title, but Marble Age's convoluted and unpredictable gameplay is what ruins everything about it.
To put it short, I have never seen a game this unbalanced. The progression of numbers (e.g. resources being required, your city's population etc.) is exponential, like in so many browser-based MMO strategies and other titles. But it is also so variable. Rather than being a smooth increase, it jumps all over the place. At one point you're suffocating, your city can't grow anymore, your tech research ground to a halt and you're passing turn after turn just to regain some military power. Then, you complete a goal and suddenly you have twice as much population as you had a moment ago, tons of new resources and several free technology levels. This pattern repeats from time to time, though you never really see it coming. It means that all the strategy goes to trash since the real way to progress is to fulfill whatever goals you have (or count on a lucky random event). What you're trying to do otherwise just doesn't matter.
In fact, the whole game is built in such a way that there is an invisible path you're supposed to be following. You don't quite know where it is, so you'll always stumble a bit. Stray too far from it and you reach a place you can't get out of. Manage to stay on track and the whole game becomes really easy. This is actually quite extreme — you can essentially lose a game if you do one thing wrong in the early stages, for instance.
(Here I'll note this isn't about following historical events or simply playing in an optimal way. The game is just constructed in such a manner that you have to make arbitrary decisions at right moments to be able to win.)
To be fair, the game does try to rescue you if you stray, giving you gifts through random events, but this only exposes the gameplay's faults even more — if the only way for me to get back on track is to accept those gifts, which are just enormous, then this just shows how big the difference between the "right" play and the "wrong" play is, even though what is right and wrong is decided arbitrarily.
It might seem like I'm complaining a lot about this subject but that really is something that ruins Marble Age for me. The game has more flaws than that (maybe I'll list some in the comments) but this is what makes it an unplayable rather than flawed title. Stay away from it unless you like gameplay that's about trying to guess what the developers intended for you to do at any particular stage.

Let's move my sliders, here comes a breakthrough! I can increase the number above one of my sliders tenfold and move those sliders again, but wait! A bad event! One of my slider has been set back to zero: I will have to move the others around next turn, until everything gets back in order and I get the next upgrade which will increase the numbers above one my sliders tenfold! Unless it is a bad event that set back one of the sliders to zero!
And I am sparing you the excitement of having to move some of the sliders (which scale crazily high) to the exact pixel they need to be, or else you'll have to cope with big letters pop-ups telling you are doing it wrong.
That's another theme of this
game: it loves to tell the player how much he is wrong. And what better way to do that than by throwing in predetermined events the player can't do anything about the first time around? Please, enjoy reading the big old dialogue box telling you what you should have been doing all that time, 'doh!'.

You can choose between two different civilizations to play as, but there is no real variety; it's the same thing each and every time.  Normally, there is a degree of randomness and variety in strategy games that doesn't seem to be present here.  While there are extra screens for managing things like diplomacy and science, turns play out on a screen that represents what your civilization is doing.  You have a certain population, and you use sliders to increase or decrease the number of people assigned to particular tasks.  Each task generates one more resources for your civilization, and new tasks are unlocked by building new "buildings".
So, aside from dipping briefly into other screens when needed, all you do is adjust resource production on the main screen with slide controls, and click end turn.  I'm not at all opposed to games that use a minimal style--my favorite strategy game is MO1.  But something about it just doesn't work here and I can't recommend it at all.
But, as with all games that have demos, I recommend you try it for yourself and see if you like it.  I ended up buying it because it was heavily discounted and I wanted to see if the game improved.  I don't hate it, but I don't particularly like it either.

There's not much I can say about this game, since it's not just essentially, but LITERALLY a glorified flash-game, but I will make an effort at pointing out just how miserably bad it really is.
First of all, the gameplay. Wait... gameplay? I didn't even know this game HAD any gameplay! Yeah, no, to be serious, the essentially only thing you do in this game is to assign/reassign your villagers to different tasks. That's it. No, really, that's it!
Okay, sure, you can "research" some new "technologies", but unlike tech-trees in actual games such as Civilization or Endless Space, the ONLY thing the so-called "technology" in this game does is to raise the amount of villagers you can have, and how many villagers you can assign to specific tasks.
But frankly, that's about as substantial of an addition to the game's overall value as a single, paper-thin slice of cucumber is to a foot-long sub. In other words, none at all.
Then there's the fact that despite the seemingly "culture neutral" nature of the name, you can ONLY play as the greeks. No foolin'. And unlike certain other greek-centric games, like Master of Olympus: Zeus, you don't get to explore greek myth, culture, legends or hell, even architecture!
No, you pick between Spartans or Athenians, and then depending on which one you picked, you either prepare to go to war against literally every single foreign party you encounter, or ragequit to the main menu and restart as the Spartans after losing 80% of your population after the first raiding party when you're the Athenians.
The insanely poor balance between the two barely even functionally different "factions" you can play as is laughable at best, and borderline depression-inducingly tragic at worst. Spartans get an invaluable military bonus, and the Athenians get just about bugger-it-up-the-ärse-all by comparison.
Adding insult to insult and injury (that is, twice the insult to once the injury), the game has literally zero replayability. The game-world is STRICTLY pre-determined, down to what foreign parties you encounter, and their so-called "personalities".
If you can't have the mind-implodingly vast random-factor complexity of the Civilization series as a whole boasts, then that's fine, but really, if you're going to make us PAY for your shïtty game, then at LEAST give us ANY kind of incentive to play it for more than an hour, and then thank GabeN for the refund policy on Steam, simply because we could play better games literally for free on any flash-games site that's ever existed since before the words "Call of Duty" was any more than an actual military term. 0/10

I picked this up because it looked fun from screenshots.I wasn't wrong.Pre-Civilization Marble Age is a rather simplistic turn based historical simulation game.It took me 90 minutes to go from Athens to being the Byzantine Empire and winning the game culturally.
The game is easy to learn and in a short amount of time you'll know what you are doing.Even if it is simplistic,it has depth and you can approach the gameplay differently.You can either be a diplomat,trader or a warmonger.
Diplomacy in this game was surprinsingly good.I didn't expect much from it,but it has enough options to make it interesting.Even if I was surprised by it,I found it lacking because it is way too easy to form an alliance,and the city states/civilizations don't have relations between themselves.
Trading is simple.You choose what you want to buy/sell and select the number of ships you want to allocate to that trade.
Battles are nothing special.It isn't like in CIV games where you control your army and so on.Your job is to build soldiers/make alliances and then attack someone.A window will pop up with the estimation of the fight and you can choose to flee or engange in battle.
What is fun about this game is the random scenarios that pop up.It's a historical game that respects the history.You play as either Sparta or Athens and you are faced with various challenges like natural disasters,plagues,Persian invasion,Roman territorial expansion,Hunnic invasion,Arab territorial expansion,various barbaric tribes invading and so on.
Once a scenario like that threatens your city/empire,you are given some choices and depending on your judgement,you will exit the crisis better or worse.
Graphics are caroonish and pleasing to the eye,the UI can be adjusted and the main menu is also lacking but good enough to get the job done.
Pre-Civilization Marble Age has some weaknesses in terms of diplomacy,replayability and balance(some civs,cities are absurdly strong when it comes to army)but even in its current state,I think it is worth a shot for the ones passionate about those kind of games.
I can see this game becoming very good with some updates,tweaks in terms of balance and even some DLCs.

This game is charming and simple, but has a lot to offer beneath the surface and is surprisingly challenging.
You start with just a few villagers and have to manage resources via sliders similar to Democracy, the first main goal is to keep a balanced economy capable of growth. As you play you'll research various upgrade paths that can unlock new buildings and improve your economy and army.
Occasionally you'll be presented with a challenge, often the challenges will test your military and your economy, and often failing them still allows you to play albeit with penalties.
As you play you get scouts that can explore the world, and settlers that can build extra colonies to provide bonuses to your capital. As you uncover other civilizations, you can make peace with them which allows for trade, form alliances with them which helps your army during military events, and eventually buy land from them which can increase your population capacity. Alternately, if your army is big enough and buffed enough and you have a few generals, you can conquer them.
As you expand and unify Greece and Mesopotamia, you'll get to decide whether to form an empire or kingdom, and the world map will expand, what started centered around Greece becomes centered around all of western Europe, north Africa, and the middle east, and you encounter whole other civilizations. There are a variety of choices you get to make which can impact how you win, or lose, the game.
Overall I'd say this is a great casual game, it's simple but endearing, and considering how cheap it is you could get a really good deal for your money.

A lot of talk is spread about hardcore gamers and casual ones. Some seem to really dislike casual games just because they are just that, casual. My opinion? A game can be "casual" and still be a solid experience as long as it does it's idea well. Peggle is one of those examples. From the get-go it's pleasant to look at and the sounds and music are satisfiying. The gameplay is simple. Fire a ball and try to hit all 25 pegs with only 10 balls. Yup, that's it. You do get diffrent powers from the characters availble, which vary on it's usefulness depending on the level. You can also get more shots by building points with one ball.
When it's all said and done, this is simple and fun. And that's all it needs to be. It also has plenty of content to keep you busy for a while. As for the cons, some of the powers are uninteresting. Tula for example gets rid of 20% of the orange pegs, and I only found a use for that power in the challenge mode levels with more orange pegs. Make no mistake about it, this game is also one of the most ridiculously challenging puzzle games out there. More challenging than trying to find the G spot on a grizzly bear with the lights off, more challenging than trying to round up people at a sleep walkers convention, yes even more challenging than trying to keep a straight face when your spouse says "do I look fat in these jeans?"
Seriously so Hard-core is this game for those that like to 100% things, that nothing less than perfect skilled shot marksmanship will suffice. The casual side of the game only requires you to clear 25 orange pegs from 100 blue pegs placed in an assortment of novelty positions in correspondence to each levels background picture. Out of the 55 levels from the game's main "Adventure" mode, each level requires you to skilfully aim 1 of 10 balls from a ball launcher placed in the middle at the top of the screen and try and get all the orange pegs without losing all the balls at the bottom of the screen. To accomplish this it is crucial to either hit a number of orange pegs with each shot, hit 1 of the 2 green peggle masters pegs placed on the screen allowing you a special ball super power, or get the ball to be retrieved in a ball catcher which moves horizontally at the bottom of the screen. Failure to clear the board of all orange pegs will require the player to restart the level, while completing this objective will offcourse allow the player to progress forward to the next level.
Every five levels you will be introduced to a new peggle master, a cartoon character with a smile as wide as the Mariana Trench that can help the player with its unique special ability when the green pegs are struck. There is also a potential for the award of an extra ball if a high score is achieved with each shot. There are a number of ways to accomplish this… hit a large number of pegs on a given turn, strike two orange pegs quite some distance from each other, or hit a purple score multiplier peg.
Hard-core gamers though will be much more interested in the challenge mode requiring players to complete levels under strict excruciating requirements, for instance trying to score 750,000 on one level alone, or to beat the very tricky ai. Peggle Deluxe is one of my favorite casual games and one of the few things EA could ever not mess up. Fun for all ages and a blessing for your wallet, this is definitely something you should check out if you're into casual experiences.
Story: As to be expected from a game like this, the story is quite minimal and unimportant. You play as a peggle student on their way to becoming a master at the game. Each time you pass through a phase of the game, you'll be instructed by a new professor who will give you a new power up in addition to levels. To be completely honest, while the story certainly doesn't ruin the game, it would be better off without it as there is no great conflict or question that drives the protagonist forward.
Overall Score for Story: 6/10
Gameplay: The gameplay is very simplistic yet requires much good strategy and sharp thinking. In each course, orange pegs are scattered randomly throughout a series of blue pegs. Eliminating the orange is how you pass each stage and you get additional points for any extra balls, combos, or extra score holes at the end of a successful completion of a stage. To do this you must aim and fire balls at each of them, lining up your shots so that each hits as many orange pegs as possible. Aiding you in you're peg massacre are a set of power-ups, each with their own perks and themes. As you progress through the game, you'll unlock more of these special abilities and eventually unlock them for all levels in the game including the late game challenge stages. All in all, this game is pretty fun whether you're in a 5 minute play session or an hour.
Overall Score for Gameplay: 9/10
Characters: The characters in this game reflect the same problems that the story does: their unnecessary and don't add too much. However they are quirky and colorful enough to add a little something unlike the overall "story". On top of this they teach you how to use the power ups instead of giving you a boring tutorial so thats a plus.
Overall Score for Characters: 8/10
Graphics: The art style in this game is very nice and vibrant, while fitting the mood of the game and its levels very well. Backgrounds are fun to look at and colorful while not becoming a liability to your performance. In addition to this there are some nice particle effects here that complement the game nicely.
Overall Score for Graphics: 9/10
Sound: The sound in this game is quite nice and fits in well with the graphics and gameplay. While it is minimal it performs its function which is all that is truly required in a game such as this.
Overall Score for Sound: 9/10
Soundtrack: While also minimal, the soundtrack in this game comes in at all the right times. From a slow and steady beat during gameplay, to the blasting version of "Ode to Joy" when you take down the last orange peg, the soundtrack is all you could really ask for.
Overall Score for Soundtrack:9/10
That just about sums it up folks. While an older casual game now, Peggle still brings a lot to the table and can be played by near anyone regardless of their age or previous experience. It has a fun and addicting premise while always sporting the low price tag which is pretty great.
Overall Score for Game: 8.2/10

Peggle might look like a kid’s game but the game is more complex then what it appears on the surface and a great game to just relax to and play on the side. As you play through the game you begin realize there is more to it than just hitting red pegs and completing the level. There’s strategy, timing and angles involved for those who do the Challenge levels which I'll get into in a bit. Combo's are a huge part of this and can result in massive scores and free balls by going for pink pegs (Score boost), green pegs (your peggle masters ability) and hitting enough pegs to build up your combo meter.
There are 50 Adventure mode levels split between 10 different peggle masters and 5 master levels at the end.
The Adventure mode is designed to teach you the different "Peggle Masters" aka characters and their abilities.
Different characters abilities are better for curtain scenarios depending on what your strategy is.
There are 75 Challenge mode levels which require you to complete the specific level in a particular way, the further you progress through the challenge levels the harder they get. Towards the last 15 or so they become very hard and only the best/luckiest players have a chance at beating them. Some examples of levels I had a very hard time beating and got a little lucky when I did beat them were "Complete a level starting with only 1 ball", beat a master AI score over 3 levels, score 750k over 3 levels etc. Ones that I tried and just couldn't do are like "Score 1 mil over 3 levels, "score 750k in a single level" and "beat 10 levels in a row".... yeah no thanks. In total I beat 70/75 challenges which is good enough for me.
