It's taken me a while to get to The Ball.  There are a few reasons for this, but it's mainly because my DVD code never worked properly, so I waited for it to be out on Steam...
The Ball is an interesting game... It takes a mechanic from other games (i.e. some world object you need to manipulate to solve a puzzle / defeat a boss), and turns it into a fully-fledged game, complete with Inca mythos...  You are an archaeologist, who'se fallen into a mayan / inca temple, and with no other way out decide to procede further into the mountain..There unfolds an interesting story (so long as you find the secrets), of The Ball.  If you don't find the secrets, you get the same story, but omitting a few of the interesting personal viewpoints of the people who wrote the stone tablets...
You proceed through amazingly well preserved temples, structures, factories, and underground obstacle courses which play out like giant MouseTrap(tm), with your trusty companion, a gigantic glowing steel and copper sphere.  Your only interface with this sphere is a weird pneumatic skull gun which can either lure the ball closer, or smack it away from you.  To begin with, you feel like it's a dead weight.. it doesn't do much, except slow you down... Later, however, the ball gets certain 'powers', and the levels are set up so that you and the ball have to be in certain places to open passages, or trigger events...
The ball is huge... in-game it must be about 5' high, and made of what sounds like solid iron... When it impacts anything living (or undead), it squishes them to frags... When it collides with you, it just stops dead...  No squishing for you.   Also, you're protected from falling great heights, or having the ball fall from a great height onto you.. so the game becomes a giant game of crazy golf, with you as the putter.
The story is interesting, and slowly reveals the history of The Ball, and how it came to be in your possession. It also explains why it seems to be pivotal in the underground cities and villages you make your way through.  By the time you reach the end, the reason for the ball becomes very clear, and the ending leaves you with some mixed feelings... The same as when you flush The Weighted Companion Cube into the incinerator in Portal 2...
The levels are lush, and cavernously huge.   Caves disappear into the gloom high above you, and massive halls stretch away into the darkness ahead of you.  Laval bubbles and hisses around molten rocks, and in the deeper levels, bricks are superheated, revealing glowing mortar behind them.
The music is lovely and ambient, largely leaving you to ponder and the wondrous scale of the levels, and evoking the unusual aspects of the game.  Sounds are limited, but great in surround-sound.  The rumble of the ball as is revolves around you is great, and in a battle you can really use the slingshot to great effect if you know where it is.
Since it's based on the Unreal engine, the game is supersmooth, even at high resolutions.  The levels are mostly quite low-poly, with angular arches and flat floors.  It relies on interesting textures to evoke actual texture.  There aren't even bump maps, I don't think, so any graphics card post 2012 should be able to run it at full res without breaking a sweat.
The controls are extremely easy, and once you get the hang of the pushing and pulling, the ball becomes just as much an extension of you as the chains in God of War.. You use it to much the same effect.   By the end of the third or fourth level, you're smacking the ball into clouds of enemies with worrying precision.
Each level has a different 'feel', and it's split into two sections.  There's even a driving section, although I feel that the vehicle isn't really utilised to its fullest.
The game has a few survival modes, which I've tried, but are just darned hard for me.. I get to level 7 or 8 and can't dispatch the enemies fast enough.. I'll try a bit more after this to get those last few achievements which can only be got by tackling the survival maps.   The game has a handy in-menu achievement tally, so you don't have to alt-tab or shift-tab to get them.
All in all, I was very happy with the Ball.  Yes, the level design is old skool, and the gameplay is VERY early 2000's, with some shonky monster AI.  But it tells a great story, through some lush levels, with good music, voice acting, and a simple, but effective mechanic.    I really enjoyed playing it, and will play some more when I have more time.

I have owned this game for years, and played it
. I'd say a good third of that gameplay is from my currently-in-progress guide. If you've come here from The Solus Project, you should note that TSP is The Ball's spiritual successor. It is not a direct sequel. While you can safely play TSP without ever having played The Ball, I highly recommend playing The Ball first. Having now played both, I can see very direct connections that both make more sense, and are more exciting to find, if you are already familiar with certain things from The Ball.
The Ball gets compared to Portal for obvious reasons: It's a puzzle game with simple tools that began as a mod and became a standalone by popular demand. This is fairly light, as far as puzzle games go. You aren't going to spend hours screaming in frustration, but that doesn't mean the solution to everything will be immeidately apparent.
The Ball experiments with a few different mechanics, but doesn't dwell on any of them for too long. Nothing hangs around for long enough to get old - unless you have a distaste for Aztec aesthetics, in which case you may want to check out the screenshots above. Some sections of this game are relaxed and can be taken at your own pace. Others require a modicum of haste.
I can't quite define why I'm so enamoured with The Ball. It has a simple charm. It does what it needs to do (puzzles, adventure) and doesn't add anything unnecessary on top - but there are extra things to explore (secrets and bonus levels) should you choose to. The story isn't particularly complex, and you do have to go out of your way to learn all of it, but the basics are literally impossible to miss.
If you enjoyed Portal for the exploration and puzzles, you'll probably enjoy The Ball. If you're seeking The Solus Project 0.1, you might be disappointed, but I would still recommend picking this up on sale.

Excellent concept, bland execution.  The core concept is there, but nothing ever builds on the original push/pull ball mechanic. This game could have been a pretty awesome coop puzzle game, but it is single player only.
PROS:
-Nice idea
-Ball moves around easily and without headache (this COULD have been a major frustration point, but is executed almost perfectly).
-Voice acting is ok (for what very tiny bit there is).
NEUTRALS:
-Graphics are just barely acceptable (quality/resolutions)
CONS:
-Walking/swimming/railcar simulator. MASSIVE amount of just walking around for no reason. Areas are large and excessive for no real purpose, especially since there is very little to explore (a few secrets but thats it). No other drops, items, collectibles, etc.
-NO SPRINT/RUN.  For a game with massive amounts of walking, why can't we run!?
-Barely two game mechanics (push/pull ball and magnets in the levels that do the same). No additional mechanics are introduced over the first 3 levels (8 levels total so little less than half the game). No other items, gear, or abilities. The core concept is good, but nothing ever builds on it.
-Environments are very bland with the exact same textures over and over.
-Puzzles are very straightforward; barely require thought. Almost every "puzzle" is just push these switches in linear order.
-"Survival" mode (and all combat in the game) is extremely boring and repetitive. Just  hold the ball and swing side to side. Although a number of cool traps exist, using them is usually to your detriment as it is more effective to just swing the ball.
-No plot/narrative. Every now and then there is a tiny bit with a voiceover, but as a whole characters just show up and virtually nothing is explained. Given how expansive the environments are, you would think they could use this space to tell a story....but no, it just adds to your playtime by making you walk longer between areas.

The Ball with some pretty big flaws.
First, I'll start with the good: The environment design. The vast caves and ancient mayan/aztec/central american cities are very captivating to look at and explore. There are some great vistas in the game. Similarly, the design of the enemies is pretty good. Also, the ball puzzles are, for the most part, fun, if quite easy to solve.
However, there are a lot of problems. The first thing that hits you is the wya the game is renderd. It has a sort of "cell-shaded-but-not-really" feel to it, and it looks as if someone was toying with the saturation filter a little too much at times. But this isn't anything major, and is probably more a matter of personal taste.
One of the biggest gripes I have with this game is the level design. Yes, I just praised the environments, you would think the level design was good too, no? Unfortunately, this game suffers very badly from "invisible wall syndrome". Rather than design the areas you can walk around to not have areas you can cheat your way around, the devs simply slapped an invisible wall wherever you're not supposed to go. This is really jarring and annoying when I encounter it in a game, especially one that involves having to more around an object like the ball. It ggets so bad that at one point, thanks to a physics glitch, I had trapped myself floating in mid air, standing on top of an invisible wall, and was unable to get back into the level because it was there.
Also, on the subject on exploring the nvironment. There comes times when you try to explore the area to find more "secrets", but find yourself being forced onto the next area because you solved a puzzle or boss fight too quickly, which prevents you from finding the secrets. This is very annoying.
There are also some "boss" fights which range from incredibly easy to beat to downright impossible without dying many times first. You shouldn't have to rely on the game saving your progress on dying to get past bosses.
I would also like to touch on the story. It starts with you trapped down a hole. Fair enough, an archaeologist is bound to have that happen to them once or twice. But then it appears they have no rope to send down the hole. And apparently they need a crane to lift you out. None of this makes sense, the hole isn't really that deep, and pretty early on in the game, the player mysteriously produces some rope with which to tie the ball to things.
So in short, The Ball is a fairly mediocre puzzle game, which if you're just a new and casual player, you may enjoy, but if you've played games for a while, you will very easily spot the flaws in it.

The Ball has you taking on the role of an archaeologist exploring an ancient mayan-esque city buried deep underground. The only tool at your disposal is a small tool that can be used to hammer or to pull the game's main implement: the ball. You use the tool and the ball to solve the majority of the game's puzzles as well as to destroy enemies by rolling the ball over them. The game's atmosphere is pretty cozy and the music fits the visuals and I get kind of an early 00s FPS feeling from the controls (which is fine). The puzzles are very easy and you likely won't find yourself struggling for very long to move the ball along. Eventually the game throws a few "boss" like monsters at you but again these can be quickly solved through trial and error. There is also not much of a plot to the game unless you manage to find all of the secrets, each revealing a bit of the backstory to how the ball, and city, came to be. Overall I would recommend grabbing this game during a steam sale (it's not really worth it's base price of $10 IMO). Still, it can be a very comfy way to spend an evening or two.

The Ball is a first-person puzzle game where you can control a single giant item - the Ball - via attraction and repulsion. Using these abilities, you then use the ball to solve a variety of chambers, working your way through the game to its finish. Additionally, the Ball can be used as a weapon to take down enemies that attack you, leading to a bit of first-person crowd handling while you maneuver them into a position where you can mow them down.
In addition to the core story, there are a couple other modes, such as survival mode where you seek to survive successive waves of enemies.
The core gameplay itself is quite solid, and the puzzles are fun, if a tad too long - much of the scenery is repetative, so it feels padded and artificially stretched out. Additionally, while I found survival mode to be quite fun, the combat which is put into the main storyline feels a little out of place.
Ultimately, if you enjoyed other first person puzzle games such as Portal, you'll probably find something to like in this game. While it's not quite up to that series' quality, there's a good bit of fun to be had.

The Ball feels like an extended UE3 tech demo that's been fleshed out into a full game. This means there is a lack of real plot, narrative and character. Each new area feels like an excuse to show off puzzles or the environment rather than the story dictating locations and pacing.
Puzzles and combat are at the heart of the game and they both work together nicely with neither one taking precedence over the other. The game starts by dropping you into an undiscovered and mysterious ancient civilization buried deep beneath the earth. Of course like most ruined and ancient civilizations it comes beset with dangers; luckily you also find the ball of the title as well as a hand held artefact that controls its movement. The ball is a large and powerful weapon but also unwieldy, you can either magnetically draw the ball towards you or punch it away using a piston of varying power. Control of the ball is key as it'll be both your protector from arrow traps and monsters as well as solving numerous puzzles littered around the ruins.
Combat is bowling on a grand scale as you launch the ball towards the enemy watching as they topple like skittles; it's a great effect and really feels like it has an impact when it strikes down a horde of mummies. And they do come at you in hordes with combat often a quick affair as you fire the ball around trying to knock down as many of them in one go as possible. Firing the ball with too much power will strike down more enemies but also leave you vulnerable as you slowly draw the ball back, it's a fine balance and knowing when to fire the ball as well as when to bring it back is key to survival. Thankfully the combat never overstays it welcome and after clearing a room of enemies you'll end up with a new puzzle to solve.
These puzzles are probably the highlight of the Ball, it will obviously be compared to Portal and whilst not quite as ingenious the puzzles are still well thought out, neither being too complicated nor too easy. The majority of the puzzles require you to guide the ball over various obstacles to reach buttons that allow you to progress. The element of solving puzzles and exploring new areas as you descend further into the ruins is what makes the game.
Once you've completed the main storyline there are a number of survival arenas which are hectic battle against the clock as waves of monsters stream into small arenas as you fire the ball around and set off traps in a desperate attempt to survive the round before it starts again. They are a nice time diversion after completing the game but no more than that.

Overall the game can give you immersion, but only if you use your imagination as you go along through the caves and whatnot.
You will need a decent pc with a decent graphics card as there are areas that can tax your screen fps.
I enjoy puzzle games so this one kept me entertained. I recommend this game for you puzzle players out there.

I'd like to start this review by saying, the Ball wasn't a bad game, I just found myself bored a bit to often to confidently recommend.
The game itself functions well enough. I never encountered any game breaking glitches, never sank through the floor,  lost the ball, or had a button simply not work. It plays just fine in that regard. The ball control is a bit wobbly in terms of getting it to shoot precisely, but it's very slight, and most of the puzzles allow for that little bit of wiggle room.
The puzzles are pretty easy, and never really force you to do any huge mental gymnastics. The hardest part of the game are the survival levels and those just involve surviving waves of enemies. The enemies are easy enough to kill (rolling the ball over them) but they're a non-threat for the the campaign and appear so sparingly in the campaign they almost feel a little out of place. They aren't there as a puzzle impediment like the turrets in portal, most times (a few exceptions), they're mostly just thrown at you to be a momentary antagonist.
The story is interesting. However you only get it through finding secrets and once you've clicked out of the text screen there's no way to recall that text without playing through the level and finding the secret again, so if you miss one that's unfortunate. The secrets themselves are easy enough to find, you just have to be patient and willing to hunt around for hidden alcoves and the like. They do however have a stage selector so if you really want to play a level over it's easy to do.
The game looks nice enough. The graphics are consistent, and I never saw any graphical glitches, but the ball itself is a bit annoying. Even transparent it's very noticeable and still impedes vision to a degree. The problem there lies in the design of the ball. The ball is made up of two parts. A round solid peice, and a complex framework. Everything fades out except for the framework, which there is a lot of, causing a sort of cage like effect on your vision.
Overall the game was alright. I don't regret buying it, or playing it. If you're looking for a game similar to portal, while this is in the same vein (logic puzzler), it isn't in the same league. If you want to have some fun walking through mildly Aztecian ruins, smashing some zombies, and solving some puzzles give it a shot.

It is hard for a puzzle game to be bad, usually the best ones are the ones that are harder to solve. The Ball is a good puzzle game inspired by Portal, and it could be a very good puzzle game if the puzzles were harder. You spent most of the time rolling the ball than thinking of what you should do to solve the current puzzle. The game is not very long, every room is a different puzzle, but for 60% of the game the only gameplay mechanic is to roll the ball. Later the gameplay expands by introducing other ways to interact with the ball, but the puzzles do not get any harder. There is a survival mode where you have to kill monsters with the ball, which in my opinion is not something that should be focused in a puzzle game.

As soon as you start the game, you will notice that the mood, setting, and atmosphere are superb. The storyline is mysterious and well thought out, with interesting to watch cutscenes. The lighting effects further enhance the overall flavor of the game, and adds an eery feeling as you explore each level. The game mechanics are well implemented, but they do take a bit of getting used to, as initially, the controls may seem clunky. The game rewards you with an achievement for killing innocent bystander monkeys and even keeps track of how many you have killed, which is rather pointless and mean. Regardless of the monkeys, there are plenty of monsters to kill that will come at you relentlessly. With that said, there is not much variety in who your enemies are, but this does not feel too repetitive or boring, since you will be doing all you can to control the ball and attack them with it, and there is a great amount of excitement and fun in the process. This mechanic really isn't as simple as it sounds, and it does take getting used to and learning the techniques. Killing the monsters makes them splat with some gore and loose body parts. These moments are incredibly tense, exhilarating, and action packed. The Ball manages to put together various aspects from a few genres and implements them quite well. It feels like a first person shooter, adventure, puzzle game, slightly reminiscent of the Portal series. The level design is outstanding, and truly sets out to make an experience that is memorable, tense, edgy, creepy and extremely satisfying. The buildings and other structures are masterfully crafted and placed in the game world for much enjoyment. Simply looking around each level is an absolute delight by itself. In The Ball, there is an overall feeling of loneliness, as you must progress through the dire situation of being lost all by yourself, without anyone helping. It also manages, through its mood, setting, and atmosphere to positively produce emotions of fear, despair, worry, and awe. Being inside the various tombs, caverns, and other structures presenting a theme of ancient Mexican civilizations is truly amazing. Everything has near perfect timing, expert design, wonderful execution and flawless placement. There aren't that many bosses in The Ball, but the few you will encounter are skilfully crafted, and a joy to watch and fight against. The puzzles are all quite intuitive and requires the perfect amount of thought in conjunction with action dexterity. They are all well developed and enacted, providing much satisfaction as you complete each one. If some of the puzzles may seem a bit complicated, the designers have included a hints system that allows you to get on the right path of puzzle solving without sacrificing the gaming experience and other plot elements. Adding to an already extremely positive overall experience, the ending was thoroughly satisfying. Once you're done with the campaign, you are also given the option to go through small, new levels not found in the campaign, in the so-called Survival game mode. It is an interesting change from the campaign, but it does not compare, as it is taken from an entirely different context, and has a whole different approach. This has been the best overall experience in a first person game since Half-Life 1. The Ball is that amazing. The environments are beautiful, the game play is rich and interesting, and it never gets boring. It is also perhaps the most fun you will have as a virtual, in-game archeologist. The Ball is a truly magnificent experience.

The Ball is a fairly interesting action puzzler. The main draw is the fantastical art direction, which is heavily inspired by the Aztecs, Incans, Mayans, and even the Egyptians to some extent. The gameplay is fairly simple: Guide ball from room to room, use it to complete puzzles and defend yourself.
Every so often, the game introduces a new mechanic (either in the world, or the Ball itself) that modifies the gameplay drastically. These moments are excellent, though they are few & far between. The Ball could have been much better served if more inventive ways to manipulate it and the world were explored throughout the campaign.
The story (as presented without finding the secrets) is vague and not terribly interesting. We never learn much about the alien race aside from what you can assume from the world they inhabit below ground. The king (antagonist? protagonist?) is simililarly left unexplored and does not interact with the player at all.
All in all, a fairly fun game which just falls short of the promise of the world Teotl Studios have created.

Tell me if you know this game: it's a first-person puzzle game set in a long abandoned outpost. You lug around a special gun that has two different (but related) firing modes, and are tasked with solving various physics-based puzzles, some of which require you to manipulate a certain geometrically-shaped object. It's Portal, right? It's not, of course: I'm talking about "The Ball". The Ball *so* wants to be the next Portal game -it has all the trappings- and completely fails to achieve that goal. While Portal has a sublime mix of intriguing puzzles and an interesting setting, The Ball's puzzles are rarely a challenge and the setting is uninspired. Quite simply, The Ball is *dull*.
The game started out as a total-conversion for Unreal and, had it remained only that, I would have been more forgiving. After all, free software from an independent up-and-coming group of developers is worth the benefit of the doubt. But when packaged and sold at retail, I expect a bit more. While the controls are adequate, the puzzles are a repetitive "push the eponymous ball onto button" (often mixed with some atrocious jumping challenges) that very quickly wear out their welcome. The game environments are bland and filled with pointless dead areas where nothing happens.
Other reviews indicate that the game does pick up right near the end, but I never got that far; the tedium of the first three quarters of the game wore me out. Rumors of a few interesting puzzles a dozen levels down the line just isn't enough to keep me trudging through the characterless boredom that comprises the rest of the game.

For a game that originally began as a mod for Unreal Tournament III, The Ball is a pleasant little distraction from the usual fare of first-person action titles.  I’m reticent to even call it a first-person shooter, even though it’s won awards as such, as it’s much more of a puzzle-solving game, and players receive exactly one weapon throughout the game.  This weapon, which looks and functions like an Aztec-skinned rip of Half Life 2’s gravity gun, provides players with a means of interacting with the eponymous Ball, which remains their primary tool throughout the game.  However, both Ball and control gun are disappointingly bereft of any ominous names.  For shame, Tripwire.
As a 1940’s paleontologist working a presumably remote dig site in the deserts of Mexico, The Ball quite literally drops players into a winding cave system lined with cryptic, ancient ruins. Quickly discovering The Ball and its control device, something draws the player ever deeper into a dangerous labyrinth of trap-laden, zombie-infested ruins.  Is it an insatiable curiosity, ancient mind control, or just a rail-roaded plot? I don’t know, it’s never really explained, but the puzzles players are led to are cleverly designed, visually appealing, and genuinely entertaining to solve, so a flimsy narrative is somewhat forgivable.
Hearkening to the addictive, puzzle-solving gameplay of Portal, The Ball was actually released just prior to Portal 2’s debut, and the influences are genuine and very much intended, even going so far as including a cross-over stage in The Ball’s challenge levels.  Trouble is, with just one means of solving The Ball’s puzzles, they do get a bit stale and predictable after a few levels.  Different environments allow The Ball to perform many more functions than simply rolling around like something out of Indiana Jones’ nightmares, but most of these functions are short-lived, and don’t feel like their true potential was fully explored, especially regarding the layering of multiple special functions at once.
Combat is another of the game’s shortcomings, as it largely consists of just  repeatedly blasting and retracting The Ball back and forth like some skull-embossed yo-yo from hell.  Boss battles and blinged-out Aztec zombie waves alike (Did I mention there are lots of zombies?) suffer from this repetitious bore, which is quite a shame, considering that one of those bosses happens to be a giant, zombified King Kong.  No, I am not kidding.
At the end of the day, The Ball is a fun little niche title, and to its credit, it never really feels like it’s trying to do more than it can.  What it sets out to do, it accomplishes, and does it well.  It may only last players a day or two, but for just ten bucks on Steam at the time of this writing, I’d say those are days well spent.

I remember when I first saw The Ball pop up on Steam and I got quite intrigued. I had pipe dreams in my head about using the ball so solve almost acrobatic puzzles using football style trick shots or impressively complicated rube-goldberg devices. I didn't buy it in in the end though. However it popped up again as part of a Tripwire Interactive bundle so I finally grabbed it.
Straight off the bat I can say that The Ball isn't terrible, it's not Duke Nukem awful or Call of Duty boring. But it's not impressive either. It's a sort of safe affair through out.
No where did I find the satisfying trick shot or juggling that I dreamed up. But that's not to say the puzzles are boring. They're fairly straight forward and no one should really find themselves stuck at any point. Some of them are still pretty clever in themselves. But the main pitfalls of the puzzles (and these are major problems with the game) is that The Ball, the main focus of the game that you drag about, never really does anything but act as another way to press buttons you cannot reach. Well, that's not strictly true but more on that later. The puzzles do not really expand to include new concepts or mutations ( again there is an exception but later on) passed  ' this button needs pressing, get to it'.
There is also a strange problem with the pacing of the over all game. The core mistake is that the game gives you little to no motivation to carry on. There is quite little reward. There's no narrative to get into, no rewards or things given to the player. You just seem to 'do' and then move on to 'do' again. The game attempts to break itself up with some random and ultimately pointless vehicle sections (mostly on a rail and with one controllable vehicle) that just seem to stretch out phases of nothingness.
The problem of lacking purpose persists into Boss fights also. For example (Oh and spoiler alert. Oh wait ! No narrative! Nevermind!) at some point you and your ball get trapped in a small square arena with a cannon that shoots bombs that you activate with a button, and a 15ft enraged zombie gorilla (yep). The solution is, obviously, to blast furry undead♥♥♥♥♥♥with the cannon.  This is pleasantly easier said than done. Until you die. At which then the game spits you out back into the arena as if nothing happened and all challenge just dissipates. What was a hectic boss fight becomes just another puzzle but with a random, annoying element (that happens to be a 15ft zombie monkey). This nonexistent difficulty curve is through the entire game mind you, so it's pointless to add enemies in it at all.
But some positive points: The game really innovates for about 5 seconds near the end. With one very small puzzle which adds new elements to the game. The Ball suddenly has this fun low-gravity field sorrounding it and much of the puzzles have you throwing the ball, jumping into the field as it cruises through the air and leaping out of it onto a far distant platform and turning in time to catch the ball again. All in one smooth move. And that is cool. Then the game snatches that fun from you and says "right, that's enough satisfaction for you, into the pointless ♥♥♥♥ing vehicle you go".
If the Ball dared to change things up a bit, added a bit more personality and varied the aesthetic it would of been a killer fun game. But as it stands it's merely safe and easy.
Worth a quid or two if it's on sale. Don't pay full price unless you're a serious lover of balls.

Rolling Sun is a My First Indie Game-quality platformer where you control a rolling ball with physics, instead of a normal character, and attempt to reach the end of each level while picking up all the glowing energy balls on the way.
It's a bit frustrating at first, when all you have is awkward movement (it was often hard for me to tell if I was too close to or far from the camera to land on a platform) and a single jump, but over the course of the six levels, you gain a double jump, an air dash, and a glide, all of which kill your momentum and allow you to recover from badly-thought-out jumps easily. The powerups past the double jump are rarely required, and mostly act make the back part of the game significantly easier than the beginning.
Ultimately, however, Rolling Sun felt out of place - in a lot of ways, this sort of 3D-platformer-with-janky-physics is much more common in Unity, and the fact it uses and brags about CRYENGINE is because the unusually pretty graphics are probably Rolling Sun's strongest point, even if the art direction doesn't always hold up. Its "My First Unity Platformer" qualities shine through strongest in the incredibly broken menus, which don't remember my graphics settings, don't have sound settings at all, don't show me what levels I've unlocked until I go into the extras menu and back out, and allow me to play the first two bonus levels even though I shouldn't have any of the four unlocked.
I guess it's interesting if you want to see what My First CRYENGINE Platformer looks like as opposed to My First Unity Platformer, but I'd have to say that's not worth anywhere near $5, and the game never really becomes all that fun. I found some of the second level to be the most awkward, but beyond that, once I started getting upgrades, it was never terrible, through the end of the normal game and the first two challenge levels.
(Note: I'm counting this one as a "finished game" review, but I only played the 6 main levels and 2/4 of the bonus levels. Some sort of bug let me play Bonus 1 and Bonus 2 without meeting the stated requirements, but I'm not willing to go through levels 1, 3, and 6 again or repeatedly in order to get all of the energy orbs in order to unlock Bonus 3 and Ultime Ascension.)

As others have stated, the controls are a bit unresponsive; although the game responds to movement inputs very well, it seems to fail to respond to jumps quite a lot. In any other game this would be gamebreaking - here it is a mild annoyance.
This game is very unchallenging - it strikes me that the developer built this game with careful people in mind, while not noticing that many "difficult" segments involving thin rods that you have to maneuver past can be merely jumped through. Moreover, the penalty for falling off is very mild, so it doesn't feel like you have to be careful at all.
The fact that the penalty for falling off is very mild is necessary, though - the game is plagued by invisible-wall syndrome. The game makes a point of being pretty, but it does not allow you to explore the pretty things. Moreover, you "die" when you go out of bounds, and there are points where instead of setting up invisible walls they just sort of kill you off instead of blocking you. This flaw is made especially clear in the beach stage - there is a portion where you have to move forward, and if you're not sure how far you're supposed to move forward, you wind up dying.
Also, it's not exactly clear what spots kill you; I've fallen off of a cliff more than once only to find myself figuring out how to use the scenery to jump back to where I was supposed to be, while I've also fallen off a cliff and found myself being bounced back when my sphere was just barely below the cliff.
I didn't finish this game - it's not pretty enough to warrant more than 30 minutes of time, nor does it present anything particularly challenging.
I feel like this is one of those situations where if the developer had a team of people working on it who provided feedback to him, this game would be significantly better. As this game is somewhat clearly made by exactly one person, and given that I bought this for only 50 cents, I do not feel very ripped off. Do not buy this for any more than that.
EDIT: Upon having finished the game and having unlocked the bonus final stage, I wish to point out that the game lagged quite horrifyingly for me on this stage and this stage only. My machine is one that I would consider very good, it has not had any problems for any game I have had any desire to play.
Moreover, a perfectly amazing example of the "exploring kills you" flaw is given in the final main stage - there is a statue that looks exactly the same as the "end of the stage" statue in the background, surrounded by a shrine. When you approach the shrine, you are killed.
This is idiocy of the highest degree.

This is a game that really makes me question the binary nature of reviews on Steam. This probably not a game I would recommend but that doesn't make it bad and I don't feel it deserves a thumbs down.
This is a game that you will probably only enjoy if you like Breakout clones. I haven't played much but the basic mechanics are straight forward: move a paddle back and forth bouncing a ball at bricks. What differentiates this from other Breakout clones is the fact that the ball has a small amount of gravity applied to it. Normally in Breakout the ball would just be an aimless floating object that went in one direction until it hit an obstacle. In Ball of Wonder we get something a little different; we get curvature. If you knock a ball too far to one side of the field, it will not bounce indefinitely until reaching the blocks as would normally happen in Breakout and is usually quite annoying to wait for. No, instead the ball will lose upward momentum and return to you in a reasonably timely fashion. This may not sound like much but in my opinion it's quite a big improvement over the normal mechanics. I only wish I could increase the gravity value just a tad, as the ball is still very floaty.
I don't see myself playing a lot of this, but I support the creator's outside-the-box thinking and would love to see what they might produce in the future.

Crazy Ball Adventures is a simple game much akin to the classic Marbleblast.
Graphics are simple but reasonably clean, however, I found that some of the moving walls seemed to cause a lateral (90 degree) impact when your "Crazy Ball" was not in that plane of motion (ie. I was hit off the platform when looking at the wall vs. being beside it).
Responsiveness of controls is acceptable with just enough inertia/momentum to make things interesting for some corners/jumps.
Sound/music is decent for this tier of game, though repetative.
There is a decent number of levels to play through, but replayability is very questionable--beyond beating one's best times.
Overall this title is worth your money if you find it onsale or gain a discount coupon (I had a coupon for 90% off), or absolutely loved Marbleblast.
P.S. (Edit)
FYI, there are no checkpoints/saves in this title--if you perish you must restart the given level. This was only modestly frustrating on 2 levels (when trying to max out both time and stars) and overall does not detract from overall gameplay.

I do not need to write this.  We all know this game is terrible and that the only reason you own it is for trading cards.  This review is just an expelling of demons I acquired while playing it for the easy achievements.  If anything, I was entertained for the first 5 minutes just from sheer awe and shock of what I was seeing.
I have nearly 7 hours of game play, but almost all of it was from a failed card idle.  I got this game from a BundleStars $2 bundle.
-Christmas Themed Music:  I have no idea why this is here.  You will hear various holiday songs done in the style of nightcore and what I can only ignorantly describe as “happy EDM”.  If you check out the developers YouTube channel, shown during every launch of the game, you will see he is quite the anime dweeb.  While that explains the genre… I still don’t get the Christmas music?  Nothing else about this game seems Christmas themed. The release date isn’t even close to December, and I could make something like this from a Blender tutorial in a few hours at the most.
-Graphics:  Ugly as sin.  All objects are made of fundamental 3D objects like cylinders and spheres.  Lighting effects are entirely 2D, and can be noticed as such when the music cuts out, more info on that in Audio.  I can’t really tell the perspective of whats happening on screen.  I want to imagine the ball is climbing a tower, but the perspective of the camera seems to suggest its just a flat cylinder.
-Audio: The aforementioned holiday songs and a single collision sound is all there is.  No menu sounds, no distinct sounds between hitting an obstacle and collecting a power up.  The music will randomly cut out and require a restart to come back.  The music has a visualizer effect on the textures/lighting, but does nothing to any actual game play.  You can add your own music, so I assume this is just a weird music visualizer project gone terribly wrong.  If for some god forsaken reason you want to go for a high score, you should load a steady house song that lasts for a long time.  No audio = darkness; it can make it difficult to see upcoming hazards as the game speeds up.
-Controls: I cannot fathom how you can ♥♥♥♥ this up so bad.. the game is just a simple infinite runner where the only dodging directions are left and right.  However, your ball will randomly continue in the direction you left it, while other times coming to a complete stop.  While grinding out 90 deaths for the last achievement(Play/Die 100 times), I tried my best to find a logical game mechanic or explanation for why it did this, but came up with nothing.  Best guess I can make is the game is♥♥♥♥♥♥and the developer didn’t care.  You can also jump, but…
Gameplay: Its not worth it.  There are no obstacles which you can gain enough height to jump over.  You sometimes have to jump to reach power ups, but said power ups will usually end up getting you hit if you try going for them.  Ever.  They aren’t even worth anything.  One is a healing kit that takes about 3 kits to heal from one hit(3 hits will kill you).  The other is a slow down which will keep you from speeding up constantly.  Neither of these will make too big of an impact on your score, as the game is balls easy anyway.  The obstacles hitboxes are bigger than the objects themselves, but power ups seemingly have the opposite problem of the hitboxes being smaller than they appear.
-Side Note: As you can tell by screenshots and the trailer, this game is headache inducing levels of bright flashing colors.  But for something spectacularly awful; anytime you hit an obstacle while moving that ends up killing you, the players ball will sometimes spin around the tube faster than the player can ever make it move.  Seriously, I’ve tried, I cannot manage to make the ball spin that fast without dying.  The only reason its worth mentioning is because it is especially nauseating and hard to look at.
So those of you who read this, you are probably wondering; “Why did you write this all out?  Its obviously♥♥♥♥♥♥ and we all know this is a trading card shame.  Do you not have a life?”
To the last question, writing about garbage is a hobby, but its a very small part of my existence.  Secondly, I just want to stress something here. this review might come off as nit-picky for something so plainly bad, but look at it the other way..
There is not a single good thing I could say about this game.  There is nothing I could pick out, by itself, and say was even remotely okay.  Don’t buy this for cards.  They are nearly worthless, just go form the badge from market sales.  Do not buy this for achievements.  Not even achievement hunters will care.

For puzzle enthusiasts
Luxor Mahjong basically sets you up with solving a series of 'Mahjong' puzzles.
If you're not familiar with mahjong (like I was before I began), basically gameplay involves clicking on two familiar looking tiles. You need to keep selecting the same looking tiles until you find two golden ones. After selecting the two gold ones, you will win the level and proceed with the next. The complicated aspect of this is that you can't select tiles which are underneath or blocked off by tiles to the left and right (so you need to clear the other tiles first). To assist you there are a few red tiles which allows you to manipulate the game a bit such as changing position of two tiles or showing you available combinations for a limited amount of time. The aim is to reach the two gold tiles with as little moves as possible as the remaining tiles will get added to your score.
There is an egyptian sound track that makes you feel like you were in that ancient setting. There is no story or voice acting though, which isn't a bad thing because this game is just about puzzles.
If you love puzzles (especially mahjong) then you should pick this game up, else you should stay away.

This is a simple and enjoyable game with a few little niggles, but overall I had a pleasant experience. This is an endless runner game where you control the road the character is running on rather than the runner itself, which is an interesting idea. The music in the menus (there is no music when actually playing, presumably to aid with concentration) is poppy and fun and quite catchy.
There are multiple difficulty settings for each stage of the game, each of which needs to be unlocked by increasing your character level with each time you play awarding you XP based on your performance. Each difficulty setting requires you to be a certain level to unlock, and you have to unlock each difficulty setting in a stage to unlock the next one.
This is where I had an issue; with each stage unlocking in a linear fashion based on your level, you often spend a long time on the same stage to build your XP, just replaying it over and over again on the higher difficulty settings you unlock just to open up the next stage, which can get a little tedious. Personally, I would have liked to have seen several stages open up at once to give you more options so as to not have it feel so grindy, whilst getting a certain score perhaps in one difficulty setting could unlock the next one. Then have another block of stages open up at a certain character level.
But those niggles aside, I'd recommend this for people who like to play for just a few minutes at a time or even those masochists who enjoy an XP grind. I think you'll find a lot to like here.

The gameplay in Peggle Nights is simple; drop a ball from the top of the screen in a 180 degree arc and hit all the orange pegs (And blue pegs for more points). You start with 10 balls and gain an extra ball every 25k points, or by landing it in the bucket at the bottom of the screen. Various Peggle "Masters" introduce new features such as the ball returning to the top of the screen after falling out the botom for a second drop, a blast that hits all pegs in a radius and so on.
The best feature of Peggle Nights is the music and background art. Each of these elements is done to insane levels, with the art painting a story in the background. The music is calm and relaxing, but changes dramatically to the Ode To Joy once you clear the last orange peg on the board.

I like this game quite a bit, there are much better MMORPG's with the same non target style but you don't come across as many as you think. Some pros are:
- The Aforementioned action style combat rather than tab-targeting system
- There is item enhancement and auction house (ala Archeage, WoW, etc)
- The PVP aspect of the game (May be a problem for many people but that's why the PVE server was made)
- There are quite a bit of classes to choose from (gender locked with certain races like demon gets top and bottom male and middle female, and humans get top and bottom female and middle male, so it sort of evens out.
- Quite a good amount of people for a slightly new MMO
- The skills are a bit less then most MMO's but they are easy to get as you can get most in about 3-5 hrs
- Enemy's are fun to fight and the game is quite difficult (depending on the class you choose
- You don't have to grind much unless your going for lvl 40 (good luck) really quickly
- PVP is great due to the aforementioned action style combat
- The download isn't so much so great to try out for a bit
Even thought I say it's a good game, it's got quite a bit of cons
- Graphics are not as good as most new MMO's (I don't care but some people do)
- High lvls can spam kill newbies depending on their moral compass
- The server is pretty stable but I ran into a few server glitches and some 10 second disconnects because of the server
-  I ran into a few bugs ( one including when I started the game Fluffy got stuck inside the wood of a carriage) but not that many
- Some spelling and grammatical errors
- Many things you can buy but not "Pay2Win" (Mostly cosmetics and mounts but there are weapons.
I like this game and I am still playing it, as long as my internet holds up :(. I seriously recommend you play this with a friend because you can team against bosses and dungeons, do quests, and you will run into many pvpers on your journey so having more than one person will usually grant you your win, or intimidate your opponent. I recommend it and I will hope to see you out there :)

Overall I feel that Sphere 3: enchanted world does not do very much different from MMO's that were out 5- 10 years ago. It does however manage to keep what made many of those MMOs decent. It’s no secret that some casual games on Steam can’t really fail, because they excel at doing one seemingly simple gameplay mechanic and never stray far from their established formula. Steel Punk Ball (SPB) is just such a title. It’s not complex in any way but it didn’t require that in order to captivate me. The game just like Steamroll before it, managed to combine two aspects that I’m very fond of. Steampunk and a true classic, BRIO’s Labyrinth (involving marbles or metal balls). The dev team behind Steel Punk Ball is ExclexGame and I’m pleased by their Steam debut and so far only project on the platform.
There isn’t a story to this title and it couldn’t fit one when considering its gameplay anyway. It’s all fairly straightforward. Not even a tutorial, discussing about the controls but if you have a keyboard (why wouldn’t you?), you’ll figure it out in a matter of seconds. The goal within each of Steel Punk Ball’s 30 levels, is to skillfully traverse the maze-like environments within a certain time frame. There are both obstacles and “power-ups” that spice things up, but we’ll focus on them in the gameplay section. Even without a narrative, your imagination can run wild as to why the stages and elements are obviously steampunk, yet the backgrounds feature a cybernetic look which resembles a huge circuit board. We’re in the Matrix, right? It’s just a glitch, move along now.
Unity Engine - Personal Edition, properly credited as soon as you boot up the game. Steel Punk Ball may not include any graphical settings in its main menu, but at least it ran in my monitor’s native resolution from the start and I never experienced any bugs or crashes. The lack of vertical synchronization was noticed once the Steam Overlay reported a constant frame rate of over 300, yet surprisingly, there was no screen tearing at all. I guess that without sudden movement, it really doesn’t look like an issue. Couldn’t even force V-synch from the Nvidia Control Panel so there’s really nothing you can do but hope for a patch that will allow this crucial feature. Other than that, SPB looks great, from high quality textures to extra effects such as reflections and the obligatory steam. Wouldn’t be steampunk without it!
The soundtrack takes centre stage here, since we couldn’t expect any voice acting and the miscellaneous sound effects made by the ball hitting surfaces and so on, don’t really stand out. But the OST was a nice mix of dubstep and a few other techno songs that seem to confirm our fears of cyberpunk being the underlying theme in Steel Punk Ball. Or not.
I hope you didn’t expect this to be a smooth ride from start to finish. What kind of adventure doesn’t showcase a few bumps along the road? You’ll be forgiven for thinking that SPB is gonna be a breeze, just after you’ve finished the first five levels or so. You’re in for a treat since the game doesn’t dish out its punishment all at once. By the time you’ll reach the 13th level (not a coincidence, I presume) it will become a norm to repeat stages either for a better time record or simply because the ball took too many hits. Yes, there is a hitpoint system in place. Getting from  point A to B would have been an tedious affair, if not for an adequate challenge in the form of various traps.
From hydraulic arms to circular saw blades and even rockets, Steel Punk Ball will test out both your patience and quick reflexes. Don’t give up and strive to improve your time by cutting corners and not bumping into edges all the time. Speaking of which, the earlier mentioned bonuses come in the form of additional time added to the counter. Never miss those purple time crystals when rolling around. I compared the title with a previously reviewed one, Steamroll, because they feature a distinct gameplay mechanic that makes the difference between success and failure: physics-based animation.
More precisely, that cheeky sphere which is our “protagonist” in this case. The titular steel ball has shifting speeds and relies on momentum, to get past ramps and even well-coordinated traps. Take my advice, on some levels don’t stop and think, just go for it. Other stages may require some planning ahead and delays in your movement or approach angle. You’ll need to adapt but fortunately, trial & error shall allow you to overcome any difficulties. The keyboard controls worked flawlessly, so I could never blame “lag” for failing a particular level. After each success, you’re awarded with a star rating, from 1 to 3. You’ll need 50 stars to access level 21 and 80 stars in total, just to unlock the final 30th stage.
There aren’t many things I’d like seeing either changed or enhanced in Steel Punk Ball. Some extra assets could never go wrong as well as a level editor. You can’t really argue with what it already offers but I firmly believe that such a title deserves both Cards and Achievements. It would almost be an injustice for so much Steam shovelware to posses these collector auxiliaries and a quality casual title such as SPB to skip them altogether. Please make it happen, ExclexGame.

You have a set number of seconds to finish a level, and either fail, or get rated one, two or three stars based on how well you did. Powerups on the levels increase your remaining time. I suspect later levels will require a fair bit of trial and error to finish them in time, as the size and complexity was ramping up rather quickly as I reached level 10.

This game to me has many flaws and many positive points.
We've seen thousands of "ball" physics games, in which you have to make your way through many different levels, using different kinds of weapons/balls, working your way out by timing shoots, creating your mental scheme, anticipate the position of the enemies when you have blown up one or two barrels/crates/bombs and so on.
I mean, there's a lot of these games.. physics puzzle games are one of the most played category in Flash websites and not only.
This game has some rare features: a button to speed up the level (there are balance games in which you have to wait minutes to see your ball slowly moving XD), a feature that makes your ball re-start when it's been stuck for 30 seconds and a general "lethality" that you have, so that you can drop enemies over yourself and they'll die by getting in contact with you.
But there are also many flaws. First of all you absolutely can not play this game in windowed mode, 'cos the game screens often are so big that you can't even understand where you are and where are the triggerable floors/bombs and so on. Moreover, physics here seems a little bit "random".. hence the fact that no one has still written a walkthrough XD On many level it seems that it's more a matter of luck the direction your ball takes.. or that the timing isn't so important, since you get in one way or another to the same endpoint.
Graphics are nice, but they're too much "predominant" - these kinds of games need the focus only on the player, the enemies and most of all the things you can trigger: you must see at first glance where are the bombs, where are the enemies located, which tiles you can remove in order to make your path, and this sometimes on Zombie Ballz is difficult to forecast, so you need many trial and error (by the way why space is the key for restarting and not R?! XD).
The developers are the same ones of Save Jesus, which was to me much better; many things are exactly the same, like the different balls you can use and the graphics style.. but Save Jesus was more beautiful and good looking than this one, for sure.
Some reviewers said that this one is better than the Zup! series but really, it's a different kind of puzzle games and even if you compare the two, Zup! is way better than this. This could be compared to awesome games like Cover Orange or Vampire Physics. And this one fails every contest.
But overall, it's still enjoyable and I think it doesn't deserve a negative review. Just bear in mind that if you like this genre of games, there are dozens way better.

TL:DR A fun tower defence game that has you roll a boulder at your opponent when you're not erecting defences. It's great artstyle and sense of humour really set it apart.
Full Version:
Rock of Ages is a tower defence game but with an interesting twist. You attack your opponents using a giant boulder which you have to guide down a track filled with obstacles and then smash your boulder into the gate of his castle. Your opponent also has their own boulder which they'll roll down to damage your gate. Between rolling boulders you get the oppurtunity to erect defences to hinder and damage your opponents. Likewise they can erect their own defences too.
The gameplay is fun but what really sets this game apart is the great art style and humour. The story has you playing as Sisyphus ( the guy who had to push a boulder up a hill for eternity) as he snaps and uses the boulder as a weapon.Each level you face of from an opponent from history like Napoleon or Leonardo and the level is preceded by a little animated clip which uses the historical portrait of each historical figure. They're all pretty funny and gives this game a bit of charm. The levels all reflect the historical period of your opponent from Ancient Greece to the Rennaissance and use the same style as the animated clips.
There are also boss fights every few levels which are a bit different to the regular levels and while kind of easy they do offer a bit of variation. There are also Obstacle course, Time Trial and Skeeball modes if you fancy a break from the story.
Overall Rock of Ages is worth playing if you fancy something that offers a unique twist on the tower defence genre.

Get this for a steep discount now. While it's initially fun, it drags on a bit, despite only being 3 hours, and if you're not interested in multiplayer, which I have no idea if it's still active, it's just a very short "time waster", but a fun one.
The gameplay is simple: You and your opponent build "rocks" and send them along a mirrored course against each other's castle. Your rock has health and will lose "shells" if taking too much damage, until it is ultimately destroyed. Your goal is to reach the enemy castle before that happens (and preferably before your enemy does, since whoever destroys the gate first wins). The more shells your rock still possesses when it hits the gate and the more speed it has at the point of impact the more damage you will do. Typically when not losing a shell you can knock down a gate in 3 to 4 hits. But you can also upgrade your rock with money. Give it a flaming shell or armor or a double jump, etc. The course itself as well as enemy fortifications are your bane of existence: From pitfalls, tight corners to artillery bombardment, bombs, towers and pushing animals there's enough to keep you on your toes.
The second phase of the game is building said fortifications. You may only build in designated areas and once your enemy has destroyed a fortification that area will remain unbuildable. To be honest, this feels tacked on and kind of weak. Between trying to hit the enemy rock with manually aimed artillery fire you're trying to guess which routes he will take and where you can have the most impact. Hint: Mammoths and artillery units are imho the way to go. Towers are just pointless most of the time and everything else is situational. Bombs are the worst, since they are just static and potentially only work if you can already push the enemy rock around and hopefully into it. Plus, they're also gone once blown up...obviously.
The cutscenes aren't really "fun" per se, but definitely silly and the story is quasi non-existant. Still, for a few bucks this is definitely worth the experience alone.

Ever since its original release in 2011, Rock of Ages has managed to persist in my memory. This may not sound remarkable, but consider that this was six years ago now - and also the odd fact that I never actually owned the game until recently. You see, I remember seeing its many quirky trailers, and being intrigued by its gameplay; half rolling boulders down hills and smashing your opponent’s defences (in a way that recalls the classic arcade game Marble Madness), and half tower defence simulator where you struggle to stop your opponent doing the same to you. Wrap the whole thing up in an art style and sense of humour that’s very Monty Pythonesque in its nature, and perhaps you can begin to see how it avoided being a fleeting memory, even without me ever taking to the controls to play it myself
Being memorable in that regard is one thing, however, but until I actually played it recently the question remained – is it fun to play? Well, get past the brief but initial phase where you painfully have to work out what the heck you’re meant to be doing, and it’s certainly fun for a while. Each battle sees you face off against a different figure from history, introduced in genuinely funny cutscenes which pack in half a ton of film and pop culture references to boot; a particular highlight is Leonardo Da Vinci taking part in a total rip off of The Matrix, for instance.  What follows is the gameplay process of using a big rock to smash through their defences and eventually squish them to death, which is something that carries with it the innate sense of joy that you’d probably expect from what that sentence is describing. Indeed, for the first few levels you’ll perhaps think it’s the most genius thing that you’ve played in years – but then the cracks begin to show.
For one, many of the maps you’ll be staging your attack on are just plain irritating - you’ve got some with high speed ramps and jumps that’s you’d perhaps be hoping for when it comes to seeking out high speed thrills, for sure. Yet they are accompanied by many others which are just twisty and confusing, or have architecture that saps the joy out of things. Think slowly jumping a large and clumsy boulder up a flight of stairs sound fun? If you do, you’re in for a treat - and should probably seek the help of a psychiatrist. There’s numerous occasions where you’ll most likely require more than one run through of a level just to get the sense of where you should be going, which just isn’t an optimal design choice in the slightest.
Worse, however, is the AI you face off against, which only ever maxes out at the level of borderline idiotic. For example, one battle I played saw the opponent’s boulder roll around the map aimlessly after encountering a tiny set of defences it simply couldn’t work out how to pass; another saw their boulder harmlessly rub against my defensive wall for the entire length of the match, no attempt to fix the problem ever attempted. Too often the simplest of strategies that is “build a wall of towers” actually pays off, and even when you have to get a tiny bit more strategic than that I never really encountered a level that felt difficult to any great degree. The only advantage the AI seems to have over you is the ability to build seemingly endless defences that go way beyond your spending limits – yet all this does is end up creating a strange situation where is feels like the the game's being cheap and resorting to cheating, despite the fact it barely adds any real degree of difficulty.
This, in turn, means the story mode of the game (which composes the vast bulk of what’s on offer) can be completed remarkably easy – I was done and dusted in about three hours maximum. The reality is the fun and novelty that comes from boulder bashing has lost its lustre by this point regardless, especially when all the irritations and issues above have been thrown into the mix. Think online battles will breathe a new lease of life into things and keep you playing forever? Ha! Good luck – all my attempts at searching for a battle ended fruitlessly. There’s simply no-one playing any more.
The question as to whether I’d recommend Rock of Ages to others, then, becomes a difficult one. None of the issues listed above destroy all your enjoyment by a long shot, but there’s no denying that they do detract from the whole experience a considerable amount. In the end, however, there’s a degree of uniqueness and a sense of joy surrounding what’s on offer here. They’re things which helped the game persist in my memory for so long, and the things which make it so it squeaks through in gaining my approval, even if it does so only by a small margin. Know what you’re getting into, or (perhaps even better) wait for a sale and pick this up on the cheap, and you’ll certainly get some fun out of it. It might not rock your world, but at points it certainly gets on a roll.

Rock of Ages has all the right ingredients for being an all timer in the "cult classic" category. Goofy premise, unique style, fun gameplay, and great delivery. It all comes together in a great package and niche-feeling theme. Its a really unique take on the tower defense genre. You build defenses to protect your gate against your enemy's weapon; A rolling rock. But the game also features offensive play. You roll your own rock as well. A ball rolling game is a simple concept but still has to control in a satisfying way and this does on both keyboard and mouse and controller. While there is strategy involved, there's also a touch of racing as you try to get your roll and hit in before the AI to get ahead. It makes for some great fun. But the game's faults make it hard to outlandishly praise and even make the simple recommendation difficult. It is plain fun when everything is working right though! And you get a good amount of fun if you go for all the extras and collectables or whatever they are.
The game felt really un-optimized for me as performance was lacking. Later levels with more commotion led to severe framerate drops. Severe. Even on the lowest of settings. There's people running it flawlessly on laptops so it was partial (bad) luck of the draw that it wasn't optimized for my toaster. But a quick search showed I was hardly alone and there were people even editing .ini files and such just looking for an extra frame. A little too messy and too much effort for a game that should run fine to begin with as far as I was concerned. So I just lowered the resolution and windowed it to tough out the last third of it. The story mode took me around 5hrs while going for all the extras. Solid length for such a "small" game. There's a few other modes left if I were inclined. The bosses while inventive departures from standard play and funny were usually quite clunky. They ended up a test of wills and a relief to finish rather than anything resembling a challenge and satisfaction. And the unique and inventive tower defense side of the gameplay did get fairly shallow once you developed strategies that worked against the AI well. Perhaps the depth truly lies in multiplayer, but that was never on my radar to play.
Was a great game to get in a bundle like I did somewhere along the line and I wholeheartedly recommend it if its a deal, bundle or other bargain. But if the theme and gameplay idea isn't jumping out at you, its an easy skip. Its definitely a niche audience that will get the most out of it. With its problems it probably won't win anybody over by actually getting your hands on it and playing. A book that can be judged by it's cover perhaps? I could be off base here. Gameplay:
The idea of the Rock of Ages is unique, you control a rock rolling over various surfaces to destroy enemy's castle door, the enemy has the exact same goal, destroy your castle door first. It usually takes 3-4 rocks to destroy enemy's castle door. Once your rocks finish rolling or right at start of the game, there will be a period of time where you'll be waiting for a new rock to become available, giving you time to build defense units (towers, TNTs etc.) on the enemy's road to slow down the enemy boulder, or even destroy the rock completely. At start of the game you are given a specific amout of credits, allowing you to buy defense units from those. You gain credits when you hit enemy castle door and when you destroy the enemy defense units with your rock. There are 3 keys laid over every map, after every few levels, you'll require a specific amout of keys to be able to proceed further on in the singleplayer. The keys are easy to get and you can always replay any level, and even if you lose the game, you still get the keys you collected with the rock from the map, so there's no need to worry about the key part.
In boss battles you simply are 1 rock inside some sort of arena where you fight the bosses, the goal is to kill the boss by hitting its weak point with the rock 3 times without getting destroyed by bosses' attacks.
The rock HP system is quite complicated. The base rock has 3 layers each having some amount of hitpoints it can take before breaking. When a layer gets destroyed, your rock gets smaller, and inflicts less damage on enemy's castle doors, it doesn't affect boss battles anyhow though, except for the rock simply being smaller, making it a little harder to take damage, but also to hit the enemy. There are another types of rocks that you can buy for credits, such as a rock with 4th layer or a burning rock which basically has its first layer set on fire, making it easier to break through enemies, but it can get extinuished in levels containing water, changing it into normal 3 layer rock. Your rock can also fall out of every map, but it'll just respawn on the nearest checkpoint and it won't lose hp at all, so there's no need to be extra careful.
That should be everything important I found worthy of mentioning from the gameplay, with that out of the way, I'd like to describe the other parts of the game.
Game's art:
You start at south coast of nowadays Italy's borders in times of Greek mythology, every new level, you move a bit forward in time and across the map of Europe (Borders of today's Italy, France, Spain and Portugal) , starting on tutorial fight with Hades in ancient greek times, moving throughout the levels all the way to late middle ages, fighting characters such as Charlemagne, Leonardo da Vinci and many more. There are short cutscenes before start of every battle, showing the enemies you are going to fight in sort of comic way, it's up to your personality whether you find them funny or insultive to Europe's history. Personally I liked most of them, but few of them took it too far (fighting the Plague, displayed as some sort of skeletal figure of human body for example). The design of the levels themselves was pretty simple, yet still nice. I could see a lot of effort going into design of the game's bosses. Except for some of the cutscenes, I liked everything from the game art-wise.
Controls:
I've got nothing to criticize in this part, the controls are fairly simple and work as they should.
Performance:
I was able to run the game smoothly on a low tier laptop without a single problem in framerate.
Other:
-The game also has multiplayer, but I haven't had the luck in finding someone to play with.
-The singleplayer is pretty short, a good player will be able to finish the game within 2 hours. For average player, like I am, it shouldn't take more than 3 hours either.
-Majority of the levels are easy, you can just place several elephants at the same place, and on most of the maps it will screw over the enemy rock's AI in single player, as the rock will get completely blocked and destroyed by the elephant defense units. Some of the defense units may feel much stronger compared to the other. I only found 1/2 of the defense units effective for most of the maps
-The game could get repetitive after some time.
Summary:
Pros:
-Unique idea of the game
-Almost flawless design of the levels and cutscenes
-Perfect controls
-Perfect performance
Cons:
-The singleplayer won't take too long to finish, I'd be really suprised if it took someone more than 4 hours
-Jokes in some cutscenes were taken too far
Final words:
This is a first serious game review I've ever done. Took over an hour to do. I initially wanted to keep it short, but it seems like I failed doing so. Still only tried to include my view of the most important parts of the game, so hope I did not forget anything. At the time of writing the review, the game is 9.99€ in Steam store, I got the game with 75% discount due to a discount coupon for it I had, my friend reccomended it to me. I definitely don't regret spending those two and a half Euros on the game, it was worth it. If you're considering buying the game, I would say it's worth even its full price, but if it seems like too much to you, just wait for a discount, definitely worth taking at 5€ and less. I'm reccomending this game because the idea and its execution astonished me and I enjoyed the singleplayer all the way through.
Thank you for reading this review, if you have any feedback, leaving it in the comments would be appreciated, it could help me if I'd be reviewing another game in the future.

An interesting little game that's one part skeeball, one part tower defense, and one part that age old joy of rolling down a hill as a kid. Rock of Ages is a nice pickup on sale to spend a few hours on.
The main gameplay is split into two sections: a 20-30 second phase where you place obstacles onto your opponents course (a mirror of your own) and then a phase where you control your rock as it rolls through a course, avoiding stage obstacles as well as any your opponent may have placed. At the end of the course is a castle gate, which you must smash into 3-5 times in order to break it open and defeat your opponent.
The gameplay depth comes from your rock's health, which crumbles as it takes damage, reducing it's size and power. As a  mostly undamaged rock can take down a gate in 3 rounds, but a damaged rock guarantees at least a 4th attempt. Thus you must place your obstacles in the best positions to slow and damage your opponent, while you attempt to avoid the same fate. The obstacles come in three tiers of different types, ranging from walls and ballistae to fans and income generating mines.  Choosing whether to take the damage to permanently remove an opponents obstacle or try to avoid it on each of your runs makes for interesting choices. There are also one use ball power-ups that can be purchased instead of obstacles, giving you some extra durability, power, or mobility for that round.
There are a few issues however: the momentum physics can lead to some obstacle areas entirely pointless, the morbid humor in the single player cutscenes is largely hit-or-miss, and the music ranges from pleasant to forgettable.
All in all, a game worth a fair few afternoons spent on the campaign or with a friend. Bonus points for having a story inspired by Sisyphus.
Note: this game was purchased by me for $2.00 during a sale.

If I could describe this game in one word, it would be "silly". In the next few lines, you'll understand why.
The plot/concept of this game is a unique take on the famous Greek myth of Sisyphus, a man condemned to Tartarus and punished to roll a boulder up a hill that keeps rolling back down for all eternity. In this game, Sisyphus has had enough, and uses his accursed boulder to escape and flatten all of time itself. From then on, it becomes a cross between a Ski-Ball game and a Tower Defense, in which you are sent to different courses modeled after different historical figures and are challenged to squish them. Gameplay is divided between two turns: Construction and Rolling. During the Construction phase, you can put up obstacles with earned points to slow down and impede your opponent's boulder, by either blocking the way or knocking them off course. Rolling Phase has you roll your boulder down the opponent's course (which has also been furnished with defenses), and break down the doors to squish your opponent.
Like I said. Silly.
Sure, this game can get repetitive at times, but it's still a fun little bit of weirdness to lighten up your day. Plus, every level begins and ends with 'Dies Irae' and 'Ode to Joy'. People told me this game was fun. And it was.
"Rock of Ages" is a half-strategy, half-reflex and speed reliant destruction game, where you build defenses to protect your gate, while also trying to hit your opponent's gate with as much force with your boulder as you can. And it's really fun! The controls are smooth, the level layout accomodates the different strategy and action playstyles, and the enemy AI can be pretty relentless during some levels. It's a nice blend of challenge and fun.
However, there are some problems. While I enjoyed the cutscenes, some of the jokes presented fell flat or got old very fast. Like the girly shrieks your enemy would cry before you'd flatten them. Or the pop-culture jokes that were shoved in here and there. The animation and style are great, but I didn't like the humor that much.
On top of that, while the graphics look fantastic in this game... the color pallette isn't the most spectacular. There's some good crimsons and golds and crimsons and greens for certain levels, but there are some that are really dirty, unpleasant pallettes like blue and gold that just aren't that colorful. But, again, that's my own taste.
And finally, the game can be a little TOO easy sometimes. Some levels I got through in one try, because their structure didn't stump me, but f***ed the living daylights out of the enemy's AI. And the bosses, while creative, are all very simplistic and really REALLY easy. You literally cannot die when fighting a boss, and the structure is find the weak spot then hit it three times.
Despite its flaws, I really enjoyed playing Rock of Ages, and earning what achievements I did. It's addicting fun you can get hooked on for a good weekend or so. And I'm giving Rock of Ages a 7/10.
